fullText:
In the choreographers’ new work, virtuosic movement and some green-screen magic unfurl the theatricality of high-stakes television interviews

It appears the interviewer has got him on the ropes. “For the record, I did not take part in a pagan ceremony with minor members of the royal family in which we daubed ourselves in paint,” states the beleaguered politician, caught outside Buckingham Palace with his flies undone and forced to defend himself. This is a fabrication, of course – I’m watching the scene play out in an east London dance studio – but it doesn’t feel miles away from something that could be true. And how do we know what’s the truth anyway? That’s the question in Deepfake, the latest piece from award-winning dance duo Jessica Wright and Morgann Runacre-Temple, AKA Jess and Morgs.

The pair tell modern stories with ambitious tech – film and live camera work – and often techy themes, too. “We’ve always been drawn to where there’s a crossover between the theme and the form,” says Runacre-Temple. “What gets us excited is seeing the contemporary world reflected back.” The pair scored a massive hit with their 2022 piece Coppélia, made for Scottish Ballet, which turned a twee 19th-century ballet about a dancing doll into a cautionary tale of AI automatons and unrestrained tech bro egos. Definitely not one-hit wonders, earlier this year they made their debut at the highly esteemed Paris Opera Ballet.

Deepfake is set in a green-screen studio, where the interview is taking place between a cool-headed journalist and a politician. With writer Jeff James, Jess and Morgs looked at a wealth of TV interviews, from Jeremy Paxman’s 1997 grilling of Michael Howard, where he asked the same question 12 times, to the former prince Andrew’s disastrous turn on Newsnight. They also took inspiration from the current ultra-media-trained politicos who “continually and bombastically evade any questions at all”, says Wright.

They liked the way the television interview is already a theatrical setup, says Wright. “I think there’s something fun about putting that on stage and asking the audience to engage with the theatricality as well.” It’s gladiatorial drama in smart tailoring. “It’s really high stakes; it’s win or lose for both of them,” adds Wright.

In the show, the interview will be filmed live by four cameras – then, as well as seeing what’s happening in reality, the audience will watch another version on screen with background footage edited in. We’ll be privy to the fabrication of the image and a number of possible realities. There are also seven dancers in green-screen suits who manipulate the environment but will disappear in the edit.

As Runacre-Temple says, green screen can actually look quite lo-fi – “It’s got that slightly absurd, playful, silent movie quality about it” – and it’s ancient tech compared with the kind of AI deepfakes that are emerging today. “They look so hyper real,” says Runacre-Temple. “The danger of deepfakes is not only that people believe things that aren’t true to be real, but that they start to disbelieve things that are true, and this gap opens up of doubt and scepticism about everything.” Or, as in their story, someone who has been caught out doing something they shouldn’t can insist it’s a fake image. “It’s really about the strange shifting relationship with the landscape of truth.”

I go to visit rehearsals on a day when there’s no tech in sight, bar a couple of laptops. “It’s good to go analogue to actually finish the choreography,” says Wright, wryly, counting the diminishing days to the premiere. All we have is an enormous studio and two incredible dancers: Rebecca Bassett-Graham, best known for dancing with Wayne McGregor’s company, who is playing the journalist; and as the politician, Kennedy Junior Muntanga, who has worked with Akram Khan.

The text plays in voiceover while the two dancers embody and expand on its meaning. Their quick-fire movements visualise all the dynamics of a charged conversation: charm, challenge, cooperation, accusation, entrapment, etc. The feel is freewheeling, but each movement is tightly mapped to the syllable, every flex of muscle is considered. In certain scenes with the green screen, dancers will have to hit exact marks and even eyelines on exact words “or the whole illusion collapses”, says Wright. They’re creating their own high-stakes environment for the performers, where “the dancers’ virtuosity is a metaphor for these very virtuosic performances in interviews”.

Will this battle have a winner? Can we believe what we see? Jess and Morgs aren’t giving any spoilers. “Hopefully it will be surprising and mischievous,” says Runacre-Temple.

fullText:
They offer advice, referee card games and manage players’ tantrums – we caught up with some of the volunteer profs who keep the competitive game going at this year’s world championships

Professors may be the most revered characters in the fictional world of Pokémon (apart from perhaps the Gym Leaders). In Pokémon Red and Blue, Professor Oak greets the player in a pixelated lab coat, and later provides trainers with their first battle partner; since then, each successive generation of games has introduced another professor to aid and guide trainers through their journeys. If you’ve ever played a Pokémon game, they are often the first people that you meet, apart from your in-game mom.

But you may not know that there are also real-world Pokémon professors – volunteers who help organise the game’s competitive communities around the world. Instead of lab coats, they can be seen at events wearing red Pikachu-mascot shirts labelled “staff”, paired with black trousers and shoes.

I spoke with several of these profs at the 2026 Pokémon world championships in San Francisco, California. Not only do they happily distribute their knowledge about Pokémon, but they also serve as vital staff at the tournament, working as referees and teachers, as well as event managers.

The official Pokémon website describes the Pokémon Professor Program as a “global network of passionate and knowledgable fans” who volunteer their time to help run official Pokémon events. There were roughly 300 Pokémon professors present at the 2026 Pokémon world championships, according to a representative of the Pokémon Company International. A professor’s responsibilities depend on the game they work with and their assigned role at the event. A Pokémon professor officiating a game such as Pokémon Unite might be hyper-focused on wrangling players and providing technical support, whereas a judge for a trading card game tournament might provide competitors with hands-on guidance as they navigate their first live competitive event.

Gemma Byard, a head judge in charge of making the final call on any decisions or questions that arise, became a Pokémon professor after her son started competing in the trading card game. She says that she and the other professors help ensure the integrity of the tournament, describing what goes into the day-to-day work at worlds – such as ensuring that event officials record the results of competitions correctly.

“We’ve got to make sure that all of the match slips have the correct results on them and are signed by the players to ensure, you know, that we get the right results,” Byard said. “We have to make sure that the venue is safe for everybody that’s around. We’re constantly looking out for anything that may be unsafe, or anybody that shouldn’t be in the venue. There’s a lot to think about on top of the rulings.”

Professors often juggle multiple responsibilities on the competition floor and will travel across the world to staff an event such as the world championships. When asked about how the Pokémon Company International compensates its professors, however, most people I spoke to declined to disclose details. One Pokémon professor said that the European professors are compensated with goodies, such as a special staff kit with merchandise, whereas the professors at regional tournaments in the US are paid wages; the same professor said that the Pokémon Company International helped with travel, room and board for the event. (When asked for an official statement explaining how Pokémon professors are paid, a representative from the Pokémon Company International declined to comment.)

Evelyne de Groot travelled from the Netherlands to staff this year’s championships. Like the other Pokémon professors I spoke to, de Groot worked her way up to staffing worlds after organising local competitions in her home region. Before we spoke, she was helping usher players out of the Moscone Center after the main convention hall closed for the evening. This year, she worked at a trading card game side event called Pokémon Sisterhood League, dedicated to giving women and non-binary people a chance to compete and connect.

For her, a good Pokémon professor must balance enforcing the rules with giving competitors the tools they need to enjoy the game itself. She compared the position to working in “customer service”.

“[Players] make friendships. You see them smile. You see them have a good time, but you’re part of that,” de Groot said. “If you’re not organising it properly, if you don’t give them clear instructions, then you see some failure […] You will sometimes get questions. You need to make sure you’re knowledgable regarding that. If you don’t know what you’re doing, if you don’t know how the card game works, then you can’t help them.”

De Groot’s experience as a professor has been relatively relaxed. However, some professors must serve as referees and make contentious calls throughout the competition. For Byard, that means she sometimes needs to deal with upset players. At one point during the tournament, she had to manage a player who was upset with a ruling that didn’t go his way.

“I got called over to the table, and I said to him: ‘Look, I need you just to keep your voice down and be respectful, and we’ll talk through what’s happened.’ And he was like: ‘I don’t need to talk to you. I need to talk to the head judge,’” Byard said, chuckling. “Well, buddy, you are talking to the head judge. That’s the kind of sass that we deal with a lot.”

A difficult call can lead to controversy. Earlier this year, a ruling from a different judge at another tournament made headlines when a competitive Pokémon Go player who goes by the name Firestar73 was disqualified after winning the final at the Pokémon Orlando regional championships. Many, including the competitor himself in a statement, conceded that the decision was a “good-faith mistake”.

I asked Byard about what it’s like to make tough calls at the tournament. She said that the professors are often seen as “the bad guys”. What does she wish competitors and viewers understood about the role?

“What they don’t understand is that they’re seeing a picture, but we’re getting the entire story, and we’re making the decisions based upon that story,” she said. “That can make a real difference. And we’re the ones putting ourselves out there to right a situation that’s been broken by players. We haven’t caused any distress. We’re there just to try and put it back together again.”

Interviews for this feature took place at the Pokémon world championships in San Francisco. The writer’s travel and accommodation expenses were met by the Pokémon Company.

title: What are Welsh sides' chances for new URC season?
description: BBC Sport Wales looks at the prospects for Cardiff, Dragons, Ospreys and Scarlets in the 2026-27 United Rugby Championship season.
fullText:
Perhaps it is down to the hope and excitement of pre-season but all four Welsh clubs go into the 2026-27 United Rugby Championship (URC) with dreams of making the play-offs.

Last season Cardiff were the only side from Wales to make the top eight while Scarlets and Ospreys were the sole Welsh representatives in 2025 and 2024 respectively.

Those three, and Dragons, have shown they can mix it with the best in the league on their day and all will feel the top eight is not out of reach if they have some luck with injury.

They will attempt to set the tone for the season in the first block of the URC, with Saturday's meeting between Scarlets and Cardiff in Llanelli the first of five derbies before the break for the November internationals.

BBC Sport Wales assesses the chances of all four Welsh teams for the coming season.

Wales beat the Boks and the rest of the URC preview

Behind the scenes on URC Media Day

Welsh rugby's ins, outs and re-signings for 2026-27

Key man: Teddy Williams - Cardiff will hope the Wales lock, their player of the year in 2024-25, can stay fit having been limited to three appearances in the past season after a dislocated right foot last October.

Prospects: The Blue and Blacks aim to celebrate their 150th anniversary by building on a strong 2025-26 when they made the play-offs for the first time.

After a blow on the eve of the season when boss Matt Sherratt left for Wales, Corniel van Zyl guided Cardiff to sixth in the table and Champions Cup qualification.

The South African is now charged with continuing an upward trend, helped by clarity about his future after being officially appointed permanent head coach in April.

"It does feel way better to know what is coming," said the former lock, who held talks with Benetton about their top job before they appointed ex-Wales boss Wayne Pivac.

"It helps to manage and plan well, whereas if you are thrown in at the deep end then you can make decisions quickly and it's not necessarily the right thing to do."

Cardiff's success was built on their formidable Arms Park record, with Scarlets the only team to beat them in the Welsh capital.

Expectations are high and they must mix top-tier European rugby with another tilt at the top eight, with a tricky five-day turnaround from Northampton in the Champions Cup to a home URC fixture with Sharks in October.

"Look at the last three years and Cardiff has grown. That's the main focus for us, to be a better team, and better individually and collectively as a club," said Van Zyl.

"We are not the cream of the crop yet, so the mission is to get better and have consistency in our performance.

"Last year we were very good at the Arms Park and we would love to replicate that, and also get better away from home. That's the challenge."

Derbies in the first block against Scarlets in Llanelli and Ospreys at St Helen's are key to that desire.

Cardiff will want to be Wales' top team once more.

Sio hopes Cardiff move leads to World Cup hat-trick

Wales back row Faletau signs new Cardiff deal

Co-captains: Sam Parry and Owen Watkin

Key man: Lalaki Foketi - The nine-times Wallabies centre arrives from Super Rugby side Chiefs and has the ability to prove a real game-breaker.

Wing Marika Koroibete is the more household name but Foketi can provide something that Ospreys or very few Welsh sides possess.

Prospects: It will be a fascinating season for Ospreys on and off the field.

To improve on last season's 11th place finish, Mark Jones' side must repeat the home form and their success in derbies that saw them lift the Welsh shield.

Put simply, Ospreys have to start winning more away games if they want to launch a play-off push, and they start their season in South Africa against Sharks and Lions.

"We had seven wins and two draws last season and 10 wins would normally get you in the play-offs," said Ospreys head coach Jones.

"We know we are not a million miles away and we have been in and around the play-offs and we want to be in there competing this season."

Ospreylia: How Welsh club turned to a land down under

Resilient Ospreys players need certainty - Jones

Ospreys have launched a recruitment drive in Australia with three Wallabies arriving in back-row forward Liam Wright, centre Foketi and wing Koroibete.

Australian fly-half Lawson Creighton has also come in to go alongside lock Ryan Smith, who was a resounding success last season.

It is policy that has excited supporters after the loss of Wales captains Jac Morgan and Dewi Lake, but one that is happening amid uncertainty over the club's future with the Welsh Rugby Union (WRU) getting rid of a west Wales region in 2028.

The Ospreys, aided by Swansea Council, hope to secure the long-term future and to do this by moving into their new seaside St Helen's home, while Wales legend Alun Wyn Jones has joined the board.

The opening home game is against the Dragons on 24 October and the Ospreys' faithful have one final major chance to demonstrate they will back their team. A successful start to the season will help that quest.

"Having your own home is massive," said Mark Jones. "The Swansea.com Stadium and Bridgend were great, but this gives us the opportunity to bring the city and the rest of the region in."

Director of rugby: Nigel Davies

Key man: Fletcher Anderson - The number eight from New Zealand was the Welsh signing of the season last year with his powerful bursts. Once he recovers from a groin injury, Anderson will aim to avoid suffering the dreaded second season syndrome against teams that now know what he can do.

Prospects: Scarlets players and fans will expect a noticeable improvement from last season. No Champions Cup victories and 14th place in the URC was not acceptable for a side that is the most recent Welsh team to win the league in 2017.

Nigel Davies has become the permanent director of rugby with Dwayne Peel continuing as head coach.

"We were absolutely not happy with 14th," said Davies.

"I'm not going to sit here and give any predictions of where we're going to finish, but what we're going to see is a Scarlets team with intent, wanting to play quickly, wanting to excite our crowd and be hugely competitive and abrasive."

Scarlets have lost international forwards Marnus van der Merwe, Alec Hepburn and Jake Ball.

The main new signing is one-cap All Blacks flanker Cullen Grace who does not arrive until October. Scarlets will hope he has the same impact as his fellow New Zealander Anderson.

"We've had an honest review of where we were," said Davies.

"There's been a lot of work behind the scenes, a lot of detail, and we've put a lot of new processes in place.

"We've brought in new coaches and some new players. I know they're not all available at the moment, but that will come."

With doubts over the region's long-term future as the WRU prepares to cut a men's professional side by 2028, all eyes will be on the team's performances this season.

Scarlets ready to come out fighting for future

Scarlets vow to remain at heart of west Wales

Co-captains: Ben Carter and Angus O'Brien

Key man: Ryan Woodman - The loss of number eight Aaron Wainwright to Leicester is huge but the blind-side flanker can help soften the blow. After facing Barbarians with Wales last summer, the uncapped forward can put himself in the mix for the World Cup.

Prospects: Dragons' much-improved 2025-26 has led to them setting a lofty target of being in the mix for the play-offs.

Filo Tiatia's side made the semi-finals of the Challenge Cup and had the biggest points swing in the URC, claiming 28 after the previous year's embarrassing tally of nine.

After four draws, Dragons feel that they can push into the race for the top eight.

They will at least want to avoid being Wales' lowest-ranked side - something they have been in 18 of 23 seasons - and end their 21-game losing streak against closest rivals Cardiff that goes back to 2015.

Dragons have made just three signings and only one of them, Tonga wing Anzelo Tu'itavuki, will feature in the first block of the season.

After plenty of summers of upheaval, influential centre Aneurin Owen sees the lack of change as a positive.

"It has meant we have been able to build on last season, we've not started from scratch," he said.

"Changes can be good but they can also be disruptive. We have banked all of the stuff from last season and been able to develop our game a lot more."

Dragons travel to Benetton but then play five fixtures in Wales before the break for the Nations Championship.

They have home URC derbies against Scarlets and Ospreys, a Challenge Cup opener against Perpignan, an away fixture against Ospreys at the revamped St Helen's and then a Newport fixture versus Zebre.

"Last year it felt we didn't get our season going until December when we got a win and confidence grew," said Owen.

"We need to kick on. There were some promising signs last season, especially in the cup, but we still finished 15th.

"The challenge we have set as a group is to get after it in the league and Europe, and it all starts with this first block. We can get some momentum and belief."

Tiatia in talks over new Dragons deal

Your guide to Welsh rugby's pre-season fixtures

Now for the elephant in the room.

There are four Welsh clubs to look at before the 2026-27 season, but it promises to be a crucial year as to whether that remains the case from 2028 onwards.

The WRU is pressing ahead with controversial plans to cut a professional men's side.

Cardiff and Dragons are poised to be given licences, leaving Ospreys and Scarlets fighting it out to be the team in the west.

The WRU has said the process to decide the framework for the final decision will begin in December and finish before the end of this season.

Welsh players will once again be tasked with putting uncertainty over the future to the back of their minds, a situation that could well lead to others joining the growing contingent playing in England after the loss of Wales co-captains Morgan and Lake to Gloucester.

title: Charles taking record-breaking price tag in his stride
description: Fulham midfielder Shea Charles tells BBC Sport NI he does "not really think about" the price tag which saw him become Northern Ireland's most expensive footballer when he joined Premier League Fulham from Southampton.
fullText:
If Shea Charles is feeling a weight of expectation from being the most expensive Northern Ireland footballer ever his demeanour does not betray it.

Interviewed by BBC Sport NI before the forthcoming four-game Nations League bonanza, the Fulham midfielder cuts a laid-back but determined figure who is keen to play a key part in helping a young Northern Ireland side continue to build on recent progress.

Charles' record-breaking £30m move from Championship side Southampton to the Cottagers in the summer gave him the opportunity to move up a division and ply his trade in the Premier League.

He describes becoming NI's most expensive footballer as "quite crazy".

"I think I was like second or third before that. But to be number one, it's really cool. Just to be in the Premier League and just being able to play my football is amazing," he told BBC Sport NI's Stephen Watson.

"For me, I don't really think about it [the price tag] too much, and you see what a lot of people are going for these days, it's kind of crazy.

"I've just got really good people around me, living with my younger brother and my older brother, mum and dad. I've got a really good friendship group that keep me grounded."

International football, rather than the club game, will occupy the 22-year-old's attention over the coming weeks as Michael O'Neill's side face Georgia home and away, Hungary and Ukraine over the coming weeks.

Already capped 35 times since making his debut in June 2022, Charles emphasises the influence international football has had on advancing his career prospects and improving his game.

"International football has always been massive for me ever since I made my debut – the types of players you play against, the teams you are playing, you rarely got to play against them when you're playing in the Championship.

"Being able to show your level against those kind of players was always going to help.

"I feel like he [O'Neill] has really trusted me from the moment that I came in, starting me in any game that he could really, and I'm obviously very thankful for that.

"I feel like Michael has given me a bit of responsibility, especially taking the armband a couple of times, so I just try to set an example, whether that's on the pitch or off the pitch, and just be someone the young lads can look up to."

Charles has played a part in all five of Fulham's Premier League matches this season, starting in three of those, including draws against Liverpool and Manchester United in recent weeks.

Alvaro Arbeloa's side sit 19th in the table, with two draws and three defeats to date.

"Whether it was with Southampton or by getting a move the aim was always to get back to the Premier League.

"It's really exciting and I've settled in really well. It's a really good club and when I spoke to the manager we saw football in the same way.

"Against Man United it was a really good game and I thought we were unlucky not to win the game. To play in a game like that so early after my move was really good."

His brother, goalkeeper Pierce, currently on loan at Queen's Park Rangers from Manchester City after a summer switch, is also an integral part of the Northern Ireland squad.

"It's kind of the stuff of dreams to play with your brother on the international stage. When you're playing teams like France and Italy and he's playing alongside you it's really cool.

"We're really close, we played football together when we were younger, we've always been best mates."

English-born Charles qualifies to play for Northern Ireland through his mother, who follows the careers of her sons avidly.

"She is dead proud, you can see on her face when you see her in the crowd at Windsor Park in particular.

"I can tell how proud she is of us and for us both to be playing together is just incredible.

"I can't remember the last one she has missed at Windsor Park. She is there all the time. She was in Italy and she tries to get to as many away games as possible.

"I told her that when I was younger [that I would play for Northern Ireland], me and Pierce, and I've definitely followed through with that promise."

Charles feels the "potential is definitely there" for the squad "to prove how good we are".

"It's a really tight-knit group, everyone gets along. Whenever any new boys come in I always feel like they fit in so well.

"When you get the likes of Ceadach [O'Neill] and Braiden [Graham] coming in you begin to feel that little bit older. It's a really good group."

title: Leeds and Warrington tussle for Grand Final spot
description: Ahead of the their Super League play-off semi-final, Leeds Rhinos and Warrington Wolves are aiming to assert themselves back at rugby league's top table.
fullText:
The final curtain on the 2026 Super League season approaches.

Leeds Rhinos, Warrington Wolves, Wigan Warriors and Wakefield Trinity remain.

Off the back of a bye week courtesy of their second-placed finish, Leeds welcome Warrington on Friday for the first of two play-off semi-finals.

But with St Helens, Wigan and Hull KR taking it in turns to dominate the domestic stage over the best part of the past decade, can two of the titans of the game muscle in on the party and seal the first spot in 3 October's Super League Grand Final?

Keighran, O'Neill & Miller shortlisted for Man of Steel

Leeds Rhinos captain Handley out of play-off game

Rhinos dominate 2026 Super League Dream Team

Leeds come into the fixture following two losses against Wigan and Hull FC at home.

Looking further back, they closed out their regular campaign with three defeats in five matches.

Asked what it would take to reach the Grand Final, Leeds boss Brad Arthur said he is not worried about his side's inconsistent run of form.

"[We have to be] the best version of us. We've seen that plenty of times this year and we've played a lot of good footy," he told BBC Radio Leeds.

"Our past couple of weeks haven't been ideal but it doesn't really count for much right now. It doesn't mean anything. All those past two games showed was a couple of things that we need to tidy up which we've done during the week around execution.

"But like the first 27 rounds, all that's done is put us in a position where we're 80 minutes away from Old Trafford so that's all we got to focus on."

Leeds last reached a Grand Final in 2022, however that achievement came off the back of Richard Agar's departure in March of that season, when Leeds had won just once in their opening six games of the campaign.

In stepped Rohan Smith, who eventually strung together 11 wins from 13 matches to take them to Old Trafford where they were defeated by St Helens - however it was an even more impressive achievement given their fifth-placed finish at the end of the season.

This year, Arthur thinks his side are prepared for the rigours of a post-season campaign.

"We're ready to go. We're nice and fresh and the best version of us, we know, is good enough," he added.

"We've got to find that and we've got to do it for 80 minutes."

For Warrington, they earned their trip to Headingley having beaten reigning champions Hull KR last week in their eliminator.

Matty Ashton scored a hat-trick of tries as they ran out 35-12 winners and that win is the culmination of what has been a consistent season for the Wire.

Whereas Sam Burgess' side have tailed off in the latter stages of the campaign during his reign, this season has been different.

Ultimately they were forced to settle for third place on points difference following their final game of the regular season and they finished the campaign with nine wins from their last 11 matches.

As for the reason behind their recent success - Burgess gave an unconventional answer compared to what you might expect from a head coach.

"As coaches we just stay out of the way. We don't need to overdo anything, we leave them to it," Burgess told BBC Radio Merseyside.

"We're staying pretty humble now. Hard work will get us where we'd like to go."

Having got through one knockout game of rugby, Burgess said their preparations to face a Leeds side they have already lost to twice this season, will go ahead as normal.

"They will be aware of that, they can't hide from it," he added.

"For us it's about going there and not giving them too much space and being clinical and playing our game."

Two members of the Rhinos' squad who will not take part will be captain Ash Handley and Lachie Miller.

Man of Steel nominee Miller has been ruled out ever since he picked up a hamstring injury in Leeds' defeat by Wigan earlier this month.

Meanwhile Handley - who had been filling in at full-back for Miller - is out of Friday's game with a back injury.

Centre Jack Bird also misses out with his own hamstring injury, meaning 20-year-old Fergie McCormack will make his his fourth career start - in a huge play-off game.

Despite these omissions, Arthur believes his side have utilised their week off well.

"We had a big session on Friday try to simulate a game as close as we could and then on Monday they bounced in and nice and fresh and looked fast," he continued.

"We've made the most of it and only time will tell. We need to make sure that we cash in on the opportunity that we've been given to have the 14 days."

Meanwhile, having missed out on a play-off spot in 2025, Warrington will not let that affect their performance when they take on Leeds according to Burgess.

"It's not part of our psyche. We're really focused internally at the moment," he added.

"I don't discuss it. They don't discuss it. It's business for us on Friday night and that's something that's working for us. So we're just going to stay in that vein."

title: Will Saints reign again or new winners rise? - Prem Rugby club guide
description: BBC Sport commentators and reporters analyse how the 10 Prem Rugby clubs will fare ahead of the start of the 2026-27 season.
fullText:
Blink and it seems like a Prem Rugby season has only just finished but it has already been 97 days since 2025-26 wrapped up at Allianz Stadium, Twickenham.

A new campaign of the English top flight stretches before us, with 18 rounds of games between now and early next June, all against the backdrop of a World Cup that is just over 12 months away.

BBC Sport commentators and pundits from across England analyse what we can expect from each club when the games get under way.

Commentary of every Prem Rugby game is available on BBC local radio, via BBC Sounds or the BBC Sport website.

Key signing: Dan du Preez, number eight

Dan Albutt, BBC Radio Bristol commentator

Bath's recruitment has been low-key with only two prime additions in South African number eight Dan du Preez and Scotland prop Jamie Bhatti, so the concern for them will be the loss of big ball carriers, especially prop Thomas du Toit and back-rower Alfie Barbeary.

Replacing their impact will be tough, but Bath still have a loaded squad that will once again have Scotland fly-half Finn Russell pulling the strings.

Last season's home semi-final defeat by Exeter will still sting, but head of rugby Johann van Graan has proven to be a master of learning from bad experiences and turning them into positives.

If they can, then they should challenge for honours again, but Du Toit and Barbeary are big losses and it may make that task a lot harder.

Scotland forward Josh Bayliss may be the most underrated player in the Prem; his power and pace will be a big asset to Bath in a stacked back row.

Listen to The Scrum every Tuesday at 18:00 on BBC Radio Bristol and BBC Sounds.

Key signing: Ethan Staddon, back-row forward

Damian Derrick, BBC Points West sports reporter

Bristol Bears enter Pat Lam's 10th season with the clearly stated ambition of getting back into the top four play-off places.

Strangely for Bears, it was their attack and lack of tries that cost them last season. A second full season back in rugby union for Wales and British and Irish Lions winger Louis Rees-Zammit, along with a stated preference for the wing over full-back, should help enormously.

The continued development and influence of Bristolian prop George Kloska, now an England international, will be key. So is keeping Argentina international lock Pedro Rubiolo fit.

The depth of their squad is still a concern - particularly in the front five and at fly-half - so they'll need better luck with injuries.

Bristol's form after the mid-season Six Nations break must also improve as it's let them down over the past two seasons.

Get that right and Lam, who appears to be under little pressure, could be in a tussle for a trip to Twickenham.

Listen to The Scrum every Tuesday at 18:00 on BBC Radio Bristol and BBC Sounds.

Rees-Zammit to return to wing for new season

Bristol sign ex-Tigers lock Wells on three-month deal

Key signing: Dallas McLeod, centre

Brent Pilnick, BBC Sport, South West of England

Exeter surprised many by going from their worst-ever top flight season to beaten Prem finalists in June.

Rob Baxter's new-look coaching team has had more chance to bed in their ideas, and aside from Australia centre Len Ikitau have lost relatively few frontline players - once-capped All Black Dallas McLeod has come in to replace the Wallabies star while Exeter look strong elsewhere.

In England winger Immanuel Feyi-Waboso, the Prem's leading points scorer Henry Slade and barnstorming number eight Greg Fisilau, Exeter possess the attacking weapons to cause any defence problems, while in Wales forward Dafydd Jenkins, Australia flanker Tom Hooper and the highly-rated Kane James they have a pack that can dominate matches.

Off the field, Exeter were taken over by Premier League football side AFC Bournemouth's owners Black Knight earlier this year – that, along with the positivity around the squad from last season, has Exeter fans dreaming of a return to the success that started just over a decade ago where they became perennial title contenders.

Injured Exeter winger Ridl to miss most of season

Exeter and Cherries share expertise after takeover

Key signing: Jac Morgan, flanker

Andrew Pugh, BBC Radio Gloucestershire commentator

Gloucester have undergone considerable transition on and off the pitch and now look better placed to shake off the frequent 'serial underachievers' tag.

With Chris Boyd on board as technical director, Rob Burgess as general manager and George Skivington reverting to his preferred head coach role, the management structure looks more able to cope with the Prem's demands.

Further coaching changes have come with the arrival of Brett Deacon (forwards) and Joel Tomkins (defence).

There have been a significant number of player departures from Kingsholm, offset by the signing of the outstanding Wales international duo of Jac Morgan and Dewi Lake; with more experience added by the return of scrum-half Dan Robson and the acquisition of physical locks Joe Joyce and Jean Kleyn.

The Cherry and Whites scraped into this season's European Champions Cup, but Shedheads will probably view a top four Prem finish as the true benchmark of progress.

Key signing: George Furbank, full-back

Andrew Rowley, BBC Radio London commentator

Last season was possibly the most turbulent at Harlequins for almost 20 years, as a series of heavy defeats led to the club issuing a statement acknowledging that things had to change.

Chief executive Laurie Dalrymple and chairman David Morgan stated that "performances and results in the men's team are not at the level we expect at Harlequins and are not considered acceptable by anyone within the club".

A wholesale review followed and there have been big changes in the coaching staff, with former Crusaders and Australia coach Robbie Deans joining as performance director to work with head coach Jason Gilmore.

Rob Hunter, Brad Cooper, Sean Long and Jordan Turner-Hall are also involved alongside Adam Jones.

Supporters will be desperate to see that some of the promised cultural changes are reflected on the field before too long, as last season felt like a line in the sand.

Injured Dombrandt set for long spell on sidelines

Long and Turner-Hall take full-time roles at Quins

Key signing: Aaron Wainwright, number eight

Adam Whitty, BBC Radio Leicester sports editor

Having covered Leicester Tigers for nearly a decade, I find myself in the bizarre scenario of the club having the same head coach as the previous season. That's only happened once since 2018.

Geoff Parling has finally brought some stability to English rugby's most successful club, but more than that he has set the foundations for a bright future ahead.

Leicester play in a more attacking style, led by the recently re-signed Billy Searle, and have developed a new leadership group including England trio Ollie Chessum, Freddie Steward and Jack van Poortvliet.

There hasn't been much player churn, although England lock George Martin and South African flanker Hanro Liebenberg will be big misses in the pack.

Lock Cam Henderson and the very exciting Wales flanker Aaron Wainwright will have big roles to play – and seeing Mako Vunipola in a Tigers shirt will seem strange.

After semi-final heartbreak to Northampton last year, Tigers looked like a team with a huge ceiling that needed to learn how to handle the big moments.

I expect them to be around the play-off race again, perhaps with those experiences behind them.

Listen to the Leicester Tigers Rugby Show every Wednesday at 18:00 on BBC Radio Leicester and BBC Sounds

Vunipola planned to retire before Leicester called

Key signing: Raffi Quirke, scrum-half

Dean Gray, BBC Radio Newcastle commentator

Newcastle have finished bottom of the Prem Rugby table over the past four seasons, with the Red Bull takeover last August too late to avoid that disappointment once again.

However, 23 new players have been brought into the squad this term (with around the same number exiting). The squad includes a mix of internationals including Argentina's Franco Molina, Hoskins Sotutu of New Zealand and Scotland duo Elliot Millar Mills and George Turner, seasoned campaigners like Rusi Tuima and Sam Graham, and returnees to the fold such as Josh Hodge and Chris Harris.

A revamped coaching team is in place under head coach Dan McFarland, with former Wales fly-half Stephen Jones in charge of attack and Calum MacRae returning as defence coach.

Their challenge will be to assimilate these new players into a competitive and cohesive team environment quickly.

The club's strapline is 'A New Dawn'. Ambitions and hopes are high but tempered with a realism that evolution doesn't come overnight.

Quirke excited by 'new project' at Newcastle

Key signing: Retaining most of squad on new contracts

Graham McKechnie, BBC Radio Northampton commentator:

For the second time in three seasons, Saints start the new campaign as defending Prem champions and they'll want to make a better defence this time around.

In 2024-25 they started as reigning champions but finished a lowly eighth in the Prem table – reaching the Champions Cup final came as some consolation, but the focus this season is all about trying to win back-to-back domestic titles.

Although they lost captain George Furbank this summer, there should be more than enough experience and leadership to make up for that, with centre Fraser Dingwall rightly taking over Furbank's role.

Henry Pollock might be grabbing all the headlines but the key players for Saints last season were the likes of Tommy Freeman, Fin Smith, Alex Mitchell and Alex Coles. This is still a young squad, but they're reaching their prime.

As always, having their key players fit at the crucial stage of the season will make all the difference, but there's real belief around Franklin's Gardens that they can win the Prem again.

Listen to The Saints Show every Wednesday at 18:00 on BBC Radio Northampton and BBC Sounds.

Saints better prepared for Prem title defence - Dowson

Pollock signs new Northampton deal in excess of £400K

Key signing: Joe Marchant, centre

Adam Lanigan, BBC Sport England

Last season was a rude awakening for Sale Sharks as their run of three straight top-four finishes was emphatically ended.

The fact that they were out of play-off contention by the January break for the Six Nations was even more damning, eventually finishing 27 points behind fourth spot, leading to the question of whether the Sharks and their physical style of play had been rumbled.

To back up some of their local talent, director of rugby Alex Sanderson has recruited a wealth of experience led by ex-Northampton and England second-rower Courtney Lawes, while there are a trio of Wales recruits in the forwards with Tomas Francis, Nicky Smith and Christ Tshuinza on board.

But the most interesting signing is that of Joe Marchant. The centre returns to the Prem after three years at Stade Francais and he has his heart set on making the England squad for next year's World Cup.

To do that, he has to play well at club level where he will fill the gap left by the influential Rob du Preez.

This feels like a pivotal season for Sanderson, who maintains the support of the club's hierarchy, to show that last season was just a blip.

The north west club will expect to compete near the top again, but the first task will be to restore order at CorpAcq Stadium after a losing record there last season.

You can hear coverage of Sale Sharks in Total Sport on BBC Radio Manchester

Key signing: Tomos Williams, scrum-half

Andrew Rowley, BBC Radio London commentator

Saracens are celebrating their 150th season and will set out to try to make it a campaign to remember as they aim for more consistency and a ruthless edge.

It will certainly be memorable for long-serving hooker Jamie George, who announced that it will be his last season - he has been a cornerstone of the successful era under Mark McCall that saw the club win six Premiership titles and three European Champions Cups.

The supporters will be keen to give him a send off and will also be eagerly anticipating Brendan Venter's return as director of rugby.

The South African set the platform for so much success in the past 15 years and his determination is likely to make Saracens a formidable opponent for the rest.

Number eight Tom Willis is a notable departure but the arrivals of England lock George Martin, back-rower Alfie Barbeary and Wales scrum-half Tomos Williams should add plenty, while the talented young players such as Charlie Bracken, Tobias Elliott, Angus Hall, Toby Knight and Noah Caluori should continue their progression.

Compiled by BBC Sport England's Sophie Hurcom

title: 'Eternally grateful' McBurnie ready to show what Scotland have missed
description: Overlooked by Steve Clarke and dismissed by some Scotland fans, but Oli McBurnie returns with a point to prove, writes Tom English.
fullText:
Nations League: Slovenia v Scotland

Saturday 26 September, 14:00 BST

When Oli McBurnie sits down to talk, one of the first things you notice is Al Pacino staring at you, a large tattoo on the striker's left arm depicting the actor in full Scarface mode. Say hello to my little friend and all of that.

"It's my favourite film," he says, on day one of his return to the Scotland fold after five long and controversial years on the outside looking in.

"I liked certain things about his personality [Pacino as the madman Tony Montana]. I liked the fact that he knew exactly what he wanted. He's a psycho.

"I don't condone a lot of his methods, but he knew what he wanted and he did anything to get it, so I think there's something that can be said for that."

It's a humorous beginning to a conversation that covers a fair amount of ground in the build-up to Nations League matches against Slovenia (twice), Switzerland and North Macedonia:

His feelings about Steve Clarke, the Scotland boss who cast him to the wilderness

The perception in places that he's some kind of trouble-maker who's not all that bothered about adding to his 16 goalless caps

The mistakes he made, the lessons he has learned, his fierce desire to finally score for his country. "A tap-in on Saturday or one that goes in off my backside would be lovely."

A long road back, McBurnie says about his years in exile, ended by this summons under new head coach Sebastien Pocognoli.

"There were times when it looked like I was never going to come back," the 30-year-old tells BBC Sport Scotland in La Manga. "The older I've got and the more mature I've got, you really appreciate these times a lot more.

"When I was last in the squad, I was a kid really. You think it's just going to always be like this. I probably did take it for granted a little bit.

"I didn't play well enough when I put on the Scotland shirt. I can hold my hands up and say that. I didn't give the best representation of me as a player or as a person and that's something that I'm here to change.

"I'm just so thankful that I've been given the opportunity to do that. I'll be eternally grateful to the manager for giving me the chance. I'm more determined to go out there and prove why I belong here."

Pocognoli has 'positive nervousness' for Scotland debut

From leaving Rangers to La Liga - Scotland is next step for Ure

Well-travelled Binks eager to make mark for Scotland

He's here now because a change in manager has brought a clean slate and fresh eyes. Clarke found it easy to ignore McBurnie's form, but Pocognoli has reacted to it.

Last season with Hull he scored 19 goals, the pick of them being the 95th-minute play-off winner against Middlesbrough that took his club to the Premier League.

He hasn't scored this season, but Hull are going well and his performances have been strong. He's favourite to lead the line against Slovenia on Saturday.

The Clarke controversy is unavoidable. McBurnie doesn't do a Pacino when talking about the former Scotland head coach, saying - diplomatically - that he "had his own reasons for what he did".

Before naming his World Cup squad, Clarke received a call from the striker, who was keen to know if he was in with any kind of shot. He wasn't. McBurnie spoke about the chat in public and Clarke didn't like it.

"I rang him and I said, 'I feel like I've been playing well' and I just wanted to know his reasoning for [leaving him out] and if there was something he wanted me to do to improve. It went the way it went," he explains.

"There were no sour notes. He explained to me his reasons and that's completely fair enough. I said I would keep performing, I'd keep trying to work my way into his plans. I never managed to do that.

"I was gutted. I felt like I had something to add to the Scotland team. The pinnacle of football to me is representing your country and representing your country at a World Cup is as good as it gets. So, yeah, completely gutted."

McBurnie has been depicted over the years as a negative force in the squad, a rumour that is never actually substantiated by anyone in the know. What you hear about instead from the camp is a livewire with a big personality. A good lad.

"It was people on the outside putting two and two together without any substance," he says. "If you ask anyone I've ever worked with in the national set-up or at club level, I'd like to think that they'd tell you that the one thing I try and be is a very good team-mate whether I'm playing or not playing."

The perception of McBurnie as a problem player - and part of the reason why some of the Tartan Army might not have wanted him back - was not just 16 goalless games but also a certain video of him trashing the Scotland set-up.

It was 2019 when he was a Sheffield United player. McBurnie was caught on camera talking to his fellow Scot, John Fleck. McBurnie said he hoped he wasn't going to get called up by Scotland because things were, er, not good.

"The video was from a behind-the-scenes thing," he explains. "Me being the person I am, I like to say a lot of things for reactions, stuff that you don't mean, funny things. I say things almost to protect myself from insecurities.

"So, being asked if I'm going to get called up for Scotland and me saying, 'I hope not', it's almost protecting myself if I don't get the call, if you know what I'm saying.

"It's something that I shouldn't have said. I didn't expect it to go out to the world. I rang Steve Clarke straight away and apologised and he said, 'Yeah, I get it, but you'll have to apologise to all the lads'.

"That was it done and dusted. I went on to play however many games for Steve Clarke after that, but it's something that gets brought up. I get why it is.

Fight for each other and defend like brothers - Pocognoli's Scotland blueprint

"I was maybe 23-years-old, an insecure kid. I've definitely grown up. I'm a lot more confident and content with myself. There's a lot less need for me to say those things and hide behind them or anything else in life. It was silly.

"I've had two kids since I last won a cap. I have a fiancee. I've lived in Spain for a year [he was at Las Palmas]. I've done all sorts of things that have opened up my mind and given me gratitude.

"I'm a different person, 100%. I still have the edge but the most common phrase I get told when meeting fans on the street is 'you're actually all right. I thought you were a so-and-so'.

"But I don't necessarily want you to like me when I'm playing, especially if you're an opposition fan. I want you to dislike me. It means I've been a nuisance in the game.

"My priorities have changed and every decision that I make now is with my kids and my fiancee at the forefront of my mind. I'm happy where I'm at now. I'm a lot more content with myself as a person. I think that's one of the reasons why I feel like I'm playing better football."

Scoring the winner at Wembley was one of the greatest moments of his life, like something out of a movie, he says. Breaking his duck for Scotland would be a massive moment.

"It's got to me at times," McBurnie says. "It's been hard to deal with. My job is to score goals and it didn't happen so a one-yard tap-in or one that goes in off my backside - anything to get me off the mark with my country would be incredible."

He's waited for these days for a long time. Pocognoli has now given him the chance he's been craving. The rest is up to him.

title: Leicestershire to appeal against 27-point penalty
description: Leicestershire are to appeal against the 27-point ECB penalty they received for breaching pitch regulations in August.
fullText:
Leicestershire are to appeal against the decision to deduct them 27 points for the pitch they prepared for the County Championship Division One match against Glamorgan in August.

The penalty imposed by the independent Cricket Discipline Panel midway through their penultimate match of the season consisted of a £5,000 fine, the loss of all 19 points earned in the win over Glamorgan and an extra eight-point penalty, which dropped them to the bottom of the table.

They were given 10 days to decide whether to appeal - and chief executive Emma White has now confirmed they will do that, on the morning of their final Championship game of 2026, away to title-chasing Warwickshire.

"The club respects the Cricket Discipline Panel (CDP) process, which is ongoing," she said in a statement.

"However, we have serious concerns about the process that resulted in the panel's decision on the charge and the sanctioning procedure. I can confirm that the club will be appealing.

"The club has instructed specialist sports law barrister Craig Harris of Furnival Chambers to advise and represent us, and Oliver Laurence of Periculum Sport to provide independent expert and strategic support throughout the appeal.

"The panel itself found that the club did not intend the pitch to play as it did and that this was not a case of cheating. Our grounds team has an outstanding record, and I am proud of the work they do.

"As we intend to appeal, it would not be appropriate for the club to comment further at this stage.

"I would ask all supporters to do the same, and to treat everyone involved, including players and staff from other counties, and those involved with administering this process, with courtesy and respect, both at the ground and online."

It means that the Championship will conclude this Sunday with uncertainty over which two clubs will drop into Division Two for 2027.

Hampshire are already relegated - but the Foxes' fate may also impact Surrey, who visit another of three title-chasing sides Somerset, as well as Essex and Glamorgan, who meet in Cardiff.

Leics 'spurred on' by points penalty - Thomas

Following the Foxes' 42-run win against Glamorgan, only their second Championship victory of the season, the pitch was rated as "poor" in match referee Ian Ramage's report.

Glamorgan head coach Richard Dawson said batting conditions had been "tough", although there were 774 runs in the match, which lasted all four scheduled days .

Referee Ramage asked for the ECB's pitch and grounds advisor Andy Mackay to carry out a post-match inspection.

The starting point for punishment for a pitch rated as "poor" is a 16-point deduction.

This was reduced to eight points at the tribunal because of several mitigating factors.

Among them were Leicestershire's "early admission that the pitch was substandard" and this being the "first rating of below average, poor or unfit" in the previous 24 months.

In his interview with the Cricket Regulator before the tribunal hearing, Leicestershire head groundsman Callum Lewin said there were "circumstances leading up to the game that were just out of my control".

They included an "unscheduled Bollywood filming event" taking place at the Foxes' Uptonsteel Grace Road home four days before the start of the match.

The exceptionally hot weather was also a reason for the pitch being dry.

A further eight-point deduction has been suspended for a year.

The Foxes have faced a summer-long battle to avoid the drop in their first summer back in Division One after a 22-year exile, having won their first promotion as Division Two title winners last September.

title: How serious is the risk of heat death in sport?
description: BBC Sport explores the health impact of extreme heat on athletes, following the death of a Fijian rugby player in Japan in August.
fullText:
On Monday, 3 August, Fijian rugby player Saimoni Vunilagi set off from home to train with his team-mates.

After the session, he was taken to hospital. A few days later, the 26-year-old was dead.

In a statement announcing his death, Japanese second division club Kyuden Voltex said Vunilagi "displayed symptoms consistent with severe heatstroke" during the training session, adding "despite the best efforts of the medical team, he sadly passed away".

Japan, like the UK, Europe and many other parts of the world, suffered severe heatwaves this summer.

In the weeks before, the daily high was between 32 and 37C. It had been a month since the daily high was below 30C.

No formal cause of death has been publicly released, but the link suggested by the club between training in heat and Vunilagi's death has caused alarm, given the increase in global temperatures and the rising frequency of extremely hot days.

So, how serious a threat is extreme heat to athletes, what measures could help and do perceptions within sport need to change?

There have been a variety of heat-related medical incidents during sports events in 2026.

Tennis players Jakub Mensik and Ekaterina Alexandrova collapsed during matches played at more than 30C, and eight runners had to be taken to hospital during a marathon in South Korea in April at which temperatures reached 29C.

Tour de France winner Tadej Pogacar called this year's heat "dangerous" during the event, while Matthew Brennan asked "what are we doing?" after the temperature topped 40C at the Vuelta a Espana, in which he won five stages.

This summer's World Cup also featured controversial hydration breaks at every match, which Fifa insisted were introduced to aid player welfare.

Many sports - including tennis, athletics and cycling - monitor potentially dangerous levels of extreme heat using the Wet Bulb Globe Temperature (WBGT), which produces a measure for heat stress levels by assessing air temperature, humidity, wind speed, sun angle and solar radiation.

But some experts believe athletes need greater protection, or the risk of further fatalities will increase.

"We have seen an increase in the number of heat illness events in rugby and many other sports around the world in recent years," says Dr Madeleine Orr - assistant professor of sport ecology at the University of Toronto.

"People assume we've seen such extreme heat before and think, 'it was fine, we pushed through, we can do it again'.

"That's not necessarily true - the heatwaves we're experiencing today are hotter than the ones in your childhood, because heatwaves are relative to the local normal, and 'normal' levels have risen."

Though the requirements of each sport mean the impact of high temperatures can differ, there are growing calls for blanket rules to be implemented across sports which offer more cast-iron protection when things become really extreme.

"Different leagues have different policies - there needs to be more of a standardised approach so that everyone just knows what to do," says Orr.

"It's similar to lightning - most people are familiar with the idea that when there's lightning near a sports event, we take a break for 30 minutes and start once it has gone away.

"We need a similar policy on heat and we need it to apply everywhere - it's easier for people to get behind if it's universal that once we get to a certain threshold, we know what happens."

One of the big challenges with heat-related illnesses in sport is convincing athletes and their coaches to do what is best for their health.

"I've got no doubt that a lot of coaches think that heat regulation is a hindrance," says Christian Day - general secretary of the Rugby Players' Association.

"And it's a tough one for the player, isn't it? Because you don't want to be the player who puts their hand up and says they're not feeling well, or that it's too hot to train on a certain day. Players need protecting from themselves sometimes.

"It's important for team staff to have a regulatory number that they know if it hits it, there's no discussion, you just stop playing.

"It's also about educating players as to what signs to look for to identify one of their team-mates who is struggling in training."

World Rugby updated its heat and air-quality guidelines in 2025, including use of a heat stress index - a measure from 0 to 250 used to determine how dangerous hot conditions are for players, with provisions for water breaks and extended half-time periods at low levels of danger, and potentially suspending or postponing matches at the higher end of the scale.

But players spend far more time training than they do playing matches.

"If this level of heat is going to become the norm, then we need central regulation and governance as to how we help clubs manage their players and how they should react to these kind of temperatures," says Day.

"Maybe there are cases where perhaps training needs to be limited in time, or doesn't take place at all that day outdoors.

"It's not a matter of trying to call people out or produce problems. It's trying to ensure the safest possible training environment."

Pre-season can be an especially dangerous time for athletes across sports.

On 5 June 2026, the Japan Rugby Football Union (JRFU) warned clubs heatstroke was an increasing concern during the summer, and told teams safety should be the overriding priority when planning summer training camps.

Heatstroke is a sudden, dangerous health condition which occurs when the body overheats and can no longer cool itself.

This can damage the organs, cause the intestines to release toxins and potentially be fatal within little more than an hour.

Symptoms include dizziness, nausea, headache, confusion and slurring.

"Heatstroke is 100% preventable, so every single death is one too many," says Orr.

"It's not the case that athletes can handle heat better because of their fitness.

"And the bigger the body the faster it heats up, so bigger bodies are more vulnerable as well. Moving that mass around takes a lot of energy.

"So while yes, professional athletes are extraordinarily fit, that doesn't save them when the issue of concern is cooling off the body."

Amateur athletes playing for the love of the game can be at risk too.

"Whatever the elite level does, we'll see it trickle down into grassroots," says Day.

"And that's why it's crucial that the elite level of every sport sets the right example because the kids, the players of tomorrow, will absolutely copy whatever they see their heroes doing."

title: England should stop trying to replicate Spain - Gordon
description: Anthony Gordon says that controlling games is not in the "English DNA" but the Three Lions could still win major tournaments if they stop "trying to replicate Spain".
fullText:
Anthony Gordon says that controlling games is not in the English "DNA" but the Three Lions could win major tournaments if they stop "trying to replicate Spain".

The Barcelona winger was speaking at St George's Park as the England squad prepare to take on world champions Spain on Saturday - their first match together since the World Cup.

England lost their semi-final 2-1 to Argentina, before beating France 6-4 in the bronze medal match.

Ending on a high meant England achieved their best finish in a World Cup since 1966.

But many have criticised the manner in which England were beaten by Argentina, after head coach Thomas Tuchel substituted goalscorer Gordon and went to a back five.

The tactical tweak invited pressure, with Enzo Fernandez equalising before Lautaro Martinez scored a stoppage-time winner.

Gordon said that he had "never felt worse", after the game and believes that the "scar" left by defeat may mean the England squad take a different approach in the next tournament.

"[The] scar doesn't have to be a negative one because it might lead us to victory in the next tournaments," Gordon said.

"We can't keep looking at other countries and trying to be like them, because we're not them - we're English and we have our own strengths which they don't have, so maybe we start playing the way we're good at."

Signed instead of Rashford, Gordon is proving worth at Barca

Gordon moved to Barcelona from Newcastle for £69.3m in the summer.

He says that the experience of playing in La Liga - with and against some of Spain's top stars - has made him realise just how different the nation's approach is to football.

He is not convinced English players can be taught to play more like the Spanish, with their intricate possession-based game.

"I'm speaking from a point of view where I feel like we are trying to replicate Spain," Gordon said.

"Because I'm in Spain, I know we have just as good players, but they have different qualities, so why are you trying to make those players the same as the Spanish players? Because the Spanish players lack the things that we have and vice versa."

England have lost two consecutive European Championship finals, and been beaten by France and Argentina in the past two World Cups.

Those outcomes have led to repeated questions about whether the team are good enough at controlling possession against elite nations.

Spain won the World Cup by beating Argentina and dominated with 65% of the ball in the final, restricting opponents led by Lionel Messi to just two shots in 120 minutes of play, neither of which hit the target.

Spain's particular style will test England again this weekend, and the Wembley hosts will look to find a response - but perhaps not by copying their opponents.

"It's not in the English DNA," Gordon said.

"I'm not sure it's something that can be taught because now I think, playing in Spain, I can speak with an educated view on the way they keep the ball is different.

"I even look at some of the decisions they take on the ball sometimes and think I'm not sure how you've seen that.

"It's the way they're built. I don't know whether it is something that maybe we can't ever put a name to, but they're definitely built different."

Gordon's goal in the semi-final capped what was an impressive tournament for the 25-year-old and briefly had England supporters dreaming of World Cup glory.

The winger started five of England's games and also provided four assists.

He was taken off 17 minutes after putting the Three Lions ahead against Argentina and says that he was surprised to be substituted.

He says that after scoring he plays "off adrenaline" and "goes into an untouchable mode of confidence".

"It makes me feel on top of the world, especially in that moment on that stage. I felt really good," he said.

"But as a winger, to be honest, I come off most games. It's normal [for wingers].

"Obviously that substitution was different but in that moment probably yeah, but in general as a winger I expect it a lot of the time."

England had battled to a 3-2 win over Mexico in the Azteca Stadium, where they played with 10 men for over 35 minutes after Jarell Quansah's red card.

According to Gordon, the manner of that last-16 victory was a factor in the players' thinking when trying to get over the line against Argentina.

The winger also suggested that the team did not match the performances that they were creating in training.

If they had, Gordon says, they "would have dominated everyone".

He defended Tuchel's "more safe and more defensive" tactics, which sparked external criticism and in-camp disappointment.

"We shouldn't try and blame one man who's obviously trying his best and trying to win the cup for us all," Gordon said.

"As players, we could have done more to take the initiative to control the [Argentina] game. I think if we do that the manager doesn't make the decision [to use a back five].

"For me, we had the best team, we had the best players on the pitch in that semi-final, and in the last 20 minutes we didn't play the best football.

"That's something the manager can't really affect from the sideline, so I think as a group everyone together should take responsibility."

title: The eel-powered 11-year-old making history
description: Primary school student Yuki Kurihara makes a flying start as he becomes the youngest athlete at this year's Asian Games.
fullText:
Primary school student Yuki Kurihara made a flying start as he became the youngest athlete at this year's Asian Games.

The 11-year-old eSports star beat opponents almost three times his age in his native Japan on Thursday.

The youngster competes in Puyo Puyo Champions, a puzzle game similar to Tetris which was developed in Japan.

Players try to clear their screen of coloured blobs by lining them up and popping them, creating chain reactions called 'dairensa'.

Kurihara beat all four opponents to top Group A and he will attempt to win gold on Saturday.

"The best feeling in the world is winning," Kurihara told the Japan Times., external "When I lose, I cry and try not to think about it too much. When the play doesn't go well it's not fun, so I want to quit. But I always come back.

"I hope to win a gold medal for Japan."

Japan's youngest athlete in Asian Games history could also become the competition's youngest ever medallist.

Indonesia's Bunga Nyimas holds the record, having won bronze in women's skateboarding aged 12 in 2018.

eSports has appeared in the previous two editions of the Asian Games, with Puyo Puyo being one of 11 medal events this year.

Kurihara says he eats eel to prepare for contests and secured his place on the Japan team at just 10 years old.

In February he beat an adult professional to win Sega's Puyo Puyo Grand Prix Final and he turned pro himself in April - two months before his 11th birthday.

The Asian Games are being held in Nagoya and the wider Aichi area from 19 September to 4 October.
