title: How Man City overhauled their squad from a 650,000-strong database
description: BBC Sport goes inside Manchester City's data team, who have been a key part of their rebuild over the past 18 months.
fullText:
Inside the confines of Manchester City's sophisticated data operation is a fundamental phrase its experts work towards: "What does it take to win?"

In practice, the motto is broken down into three sections: identifying players, evaluating them and assessing how the club could improve them, all with a view to enhancing the statistical probability of City winning the Premier League.

Last season, the club's data department projected they would be there or thereabouts when it came to the title race, but their metrics indicated Arsenal were favourites to be champions. They were accurate.

This time around, City prefer to keep their projections under wraps - but five wins from five Premier League games have prompted predictions from supporters and pundits they will again be the Gunners' closest challengers.

City's devotion to data is at the heart of their efforts to close the gap on Arsenal and BBC Sport has been given unprecedent access to the inner workings of the club's metrics machine as we uncover some of the secrets guiding their work - particularly regarding player recruitment and sales.

Their work is a sign of the times in the Premier League, with clubs across the top flight and beyond increasingly using data for transfers and monitoring their teams' performance.

At City, one of the fundamental aims is to reduce risk of any market transaction, be it a purchase or a sale.

The system they play in at their current club and how the manager is asking him and the team to play.

Once those four aspects are observed, City's aim is to understand not just how good the player is but how good he could become at the Etihad.

Since winning the Treble in 2023, City's squad has undergone a vast overhaul using this approach. Only four players from that historic campaign remain.

It is crucial to stress, however, that while data has made an indefinite impact on how City operate in the transfer market, the work of traditional scouts continues to be the primary gauge of whether they decide to move for a player.

"Data plays a role in our decision-making, but it is just one part of the overall picture," City sporting director Hugo Viana told BBC Sport.

"We know data cannot tell us everything about a player. It cannot fully show a person's character, mentality or behaviour.

"That is why we study data insights but focus on the expertise of our scouts and other specialists."

The prominence of data, however, has grown significantly behind the scenes at the Etihad.

Here BBC Sport can take you to the core of some of City's key transfer calls from their extensive three-year squad revamp - including the £116m signing of Elliot Anderson.

The starting point for any new signing is City's database of 650,000 footballers from around the world.

The next step is the brief: what sort of player is the club wanting to recruit.

This usually starts with a position, though that process isn't as simple as it sounds.

City, for example, categorise their full-backs into three types: those who are defensive, those who come inside, and those who play high and wide.

Once the club's data departments have the brief, filters that grade a player's overall ability are applied to whittle down the 650,000-man database to 20-50 names.

Juventus full-back Andrea Cambiaso is one player who has been on City's radar after the data highlighted him, particularly his ability to coming inside to build play in midfield.

That he is comfortable with both feet rated highly on the data, too.

In accordance with the data and the scouting reports it was decided the club would not proceed with their interest in Cambiaso in the previous window, but City's approach is likely to mean he will continue to be monitored.

The longlist of 20-50 names is cross-referenced with the scouting longlist. Generally there is a significant overlap between the players identified by data and the ones already on scouts' radar.

From there, further, more refined metrics are applied to rank and prioritise the longlist.

Scouts will then complete further diligence on the players to reduce the list to a maximum of about six players.

At this point, the club will complete deeper dives into the remaining players, including diligence on their injury record, athletic performance and behavioural habits.

The information is then collated into individual reports called acquisition packs which contain all the key metrics used to inform the decision on a player.

This includes a 'radar chart', which rates a range of specific on-field metrics.

For example, when Jeremy Doku was signed in 2023, then manager Pep Guardiola decided he wanted a winger who was direct, akin to Leroy Sane, because at the time they had Jack Grealish and Riyad Mahrez, who preferred to keep the ball and cut inside.

Among the criteria applied in City's brief were the following: making (running into) the box, pressure regains, take-on percentage and opposition-half pressure.

Doku's overall numbers ticked the boxes Guardiola was looking for, although the Belgian's 'making the box' score was among his lowest readings.

Since his arrival, Doku has improved this rating - an example City say shows how their data systems are helping to improve existing players.

There is also a 'utilisation chart' that records how often the player has been used over a three-year period, as well as a scouting grade that indicates how highly the traditional scouts rate the individual.

Each player is also awarded an overall "current impact score" - which predicts what impression he would be expected to make immediately on signing - and a "potential impact score" that projects the contribution the player could make in the future.

Perhaps the most intriguing reading on the acquisition packs is a player's "action value score". This positions them in a league table that includes City players and ones from rival clubs who play in a similar role.

Once the acquisition reports are evaluated, the list is further reduced to 2-3 players once City's valuation of the player has been factored in.

Data contributes heavily to the price range City believe a player falls in, and the valuation is never a single number.

A decision is then made on which player is the priority, though all players on the shortlist are worked on simultaneously in the event of changing circumstances, for example if a player becomes unavailable.

Indeed, being able to move according to the market is something the data team feel they have become adept at.

The sudden emergence of Yan Diomande last season led to City completing checks on him before he joined Real Madrid from RB Leipzig.

The club also paid close attention to Eduardo Camavinga's metrics in case Real decided to sell a midfielder.

Anderson was an obvious signing for a top Premier League club.

The 23-year-old had developed into a key player for Nottingham Forest. An added appeal was the fact he is English, and had cemented his position in the national team.

City fought off other top clubs, including Manchester United, to sign him.

It would seem, on the face of it, a straightforward decision.

But the way City analysed it underlines their incredibly forensic approach even when, outwardly, it might be considered they did not need to be so comprehensive given Anderson's obvious talents.

The fact they still used their algorithm and went through all their normal steps says a lot about elite football in the modern day - and also the limitations of data alone.

That is because - perhaps surprisingly - Anderson's metrics didn't necessarily catch the eye.

At the start of last season, despite emerging uncertainty over Guardiola's future, the club knew they would be in the market for at least one central midfielder come the summer.

They knew Bernardo Silva was leaving while there were doubts over the futures of Rodri and Nico Gonzalez.

There was an acknowledgement that replacing Silva and Rodri like-for-like would be virtually impossible, so they looked for a player who was equally adept at building play from either deep or high central midfield.

As last season developed, doubt also emerged over the future of Tijjani Reijnders - but Enzo Fernandez was viewed as the favoured replacement for the Dutchman.

Anderson made the initial cut from the 650,000-man database to the longlist - but was not high in that group. However, his metric readings didn't immediately scream out the "no-brainer" he ultimately became.

As City took a closer look, there was an acknowledgement Anderson's case does highlight some of the limitations of data.

Anderson did not score lots of goals for Forest, or consistently provide assists. Because, generally speaking, Forest aren't a possession team like City, his general metrics in their algorithm did not grab the attention.

With that in mind, City's data analysts had to consider that, because Anderson was generally playing closer to his own goal than he would at City, he wasn't getting the opportunities to impress in the final third of the pitch.

So they paid close attention to what he was doing at Forest and modelled his potential role in a City team that generally plays closer to the opposition's goal, dominates possession and has more elite players.

Among the criteria graded on Anderson's 'radar chart' were defensive regains, duel success, line-breaking passes, aerial-duel success and defensive errors.

With his reading for defensive errors, it was acknowledged that, because Forest were a transitional side, some were a result of the area of the pitch in which he was asked to operate.

He may, for example, have regained possession deep inside his own half but lost the ball because he had to play a longer and a riskier pass after being asked to play forward quickly.

In the same scenario at City, it is anticipated Anderson would have options to play a shorter pass with a greater success rate.

"Just because a player doesn't have the opportunity to perform a particular action on a regular basis because of the team he is playing doesn't mean he can't do it," said a source.

Anderson's data readings improved significantly as the season developed, which compelled the club's scouts to watch him on a regular basis.

He stood up very favourably against City's existing midfielders - and a list of rival players the club had identified as possible signings in that area.

The results of the diligence completed by City's data team, scouts and other experts meant that even though Anderson's price increased beyond what City believed was his true valuation, they felt the risk was low.

"Elliot Anderson is a great example of how the process works," Viana said.

"The data was positive for Elliot and gave us real confidence in his profile, but it was the insight from our scouts and wider performance team that helped us understand the player and his attributes and this proved our belief that he was the right fit for the club."

BBC Sport was also provided with fascinating insight into how data was used to sign Julian Alvarez from River Plate for £14m in 2022.

The initial recommendation came from scouts, and given Alvarez was not a player originally identified by his metrics, the data team had to take a closer look.

Because the Argentine league isn't recognised as one of the strongest globally, City's general data settings mean players will reach a natural ceiling with their readings in comparison to those playing in one of Europe's top five divisions.

So, City dug deeper into Alvarez's stats, and his impact on both the ball and River's scorelines.

The stats showed he was by far the best player in the Argentine top flight, and City believed they had enough evidence to say he would develop into a starter for a top-half club in one of Europe's top five leagues within two-and-half years.

The data model valued Alvarez between £26m and £40m. City signed him for £14m so believed they were signing an undervalued player.

Alvarez's projected value was £70m after three years. They eventually sold him to Atletico Madrid in 2024 for £81m.

The signing of Abdukodir Khusanov from Lens also provides intriguing insight into City's reliance on data.

The 22-year-old didn't initially make City's 50-man longlist, but on closer inspection they found while his output on the ball needed to improve, his physical data - for example his covering runs behind - was through the roof.

Khusanov's on-the-ball metrics, City say, have improved significantly since he signed in January 2025.

The departure of Guardiola and the arrival of Enzo Maresca is not expected to alter the club's approach significantly.

The key metrics Maresca looks for in a player are understood to be very similar to Guardiola's, with the notable difference that the Italian prefers his full-backs to be more direct.

Rooted in City's coach recruitment process is a certain team philosophy and way of playing, with any new manager expected to produce a side that is possession dominant, can press high, regain possession high up the pitch, produce quality chances and entertain.

That philosophy was designed before Guardiola's appointment, and the Spaniard produced the purest form of City's footballing ideology.

With that in mind, the change in manager has not drastically altered the way City's data department approach their work.

Maresca will continue to work closely with them as he looks to build his own dynasty - but much of the hard work in building a squad to last is complete.

Before City's Treble-winning season, the internal data indicators were such that the club knew they would soon need to overhaul a squad that had reached its peak.

Selling players such as Kevin de Bruyne, Kyle Walker, Riyad Mahrez and Ilkay Gundogan wasn't easy given their illustrious service and the fact they were still performing at a very high level.

Data, though, allows the club to spot declining trends well in advance - often two or three years - before a player is offloaded.

Those particular metrics help City identify when the right time is to sell a player is - perhaps even before the buying club have spotted a drop in performance.

And when those trends are identified, the club can plan well in advance.

From there the club decide whether to start embedding a player from the academy or enter the market to replace.

Ayyoub Bouaddi's arrival from Lille this summer is a prime example. At 18, City realise he isn't necessarily going to have a profound impact this season - but the club believe the Moroccan will be able to make a bigger contribution within two years.

After the Treble season, the recruitment remit at City was to lower the average age of the squad and build a set of players that could deliver sustained success.

But doing that at City comes with a catch. Because at City, the team are always expected to compete for trophies.

Lowering the age of a squad is one thing; doing so while continuing to win is far more complicated.

In previous years, for example, City's data systems identified former Brighton trio Moises Caicedo, Marc Cucurella and Carlos Baleba, who have been lauded as data successes.

But there was a sense at City that the development of such signings would take too long for them to make an impact on a team that has the remit of winning titles or assets that could be developed and sold for a profit.

City have successfully lowered the average age of the squad to the extent they now have the third youngest set of players in the Premier League behind Newcastle and Chelsea.

But with the signings of goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma, defender Marc Guehi, and Fernandez and Anderson they have added players who can not only grow with that new generation but also already have vast experience of top-level football.

City's data indicates their current squad will not peak for another two to three years - but also projects they are likely be among the title challengers this season.

Time will tell if they are right.

title: Russell fastest in Baku as Antonelli stops on track

title: Debbie Beard and Amanda Thorpe lost their husbands - this is their story
description: Debbie Beard and Amanda Thorpe speak to the BBC's Simon Jack at the launch of a new suicide prevention toolkit.
fullText:
Warning: This story contains discussion of suicide and information some readers may find distressing

Two women, united in grief, are meeting for the first time.

Debbie Beard lost her husband just over a year ago. Matt Beard, the former Liverpool Women manager, died in hospital on 20 September 2025. He is believed to have taken his own life, though an inquest is yet to conclude.

Amanda Thorpe's husband Graham, the former England and Surrey cricketer, took his own life in 2024. He had "spiralled into depression" after losing his job as a batting coach in 2022.

The two women, who had never met before, came together at an event launched by the Prince of Wales and the Royal Foundation to urge sport at every level to make suicide prevention part of its culture through a new nationwide toolkit.

There they spoke to the BBC's business editor Simon Jack, who was 17 when his father took his own life.

On Your Side, external is a set of resources available online that aims "to make suicide prevention as much a part of sport as warm-up, training and performance".

Amanda Thorpe has said previously she believes her husband would still be alive had he received more support from the England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) after leaving his coaching role. Following the inquest into his death, the ECB said it was "a profound tragedy" and added Thorpe's passing was a "stark reminder" of the challenges many face with mental health.

Matt Beard died a month after leaving his role as manager of Burnley Women. He had been in the post for only two months. When the inquest into his death was postponed indefinitely, Burnley said they were "aware of an ongoing legal process" and would "not be making any comment at this time".

Amanda: "Graham had been struggling for the previous year to 18 months during Covid. Graham didn't really like following rules and there were quite a few in Covid - like playing under bubble conditions. So he had been having some medication and therapy in his job. But then Graham lost his job and he didn't see it coming.

"He did pride himself with having been in the game his whole life. He just couldn't believe that he was blindsided by it.

"I think at least two other people were sacked at the same time, which does happen at the end of disastrous Ashes series.

"Also he was probably drinking too much and found the whole of the last trip in Covid very stressful. He then took a playful video at the end of the tour, when they had a few drinks with the opposition. One of the players sent it to two friends and someone unfortunately leaked it, so it was in the Sydney Morning Herald."

Simon: "Going for a few drinks with the opposition - you would think that that happens in sport all the time, but they lost?"

Amanda: "Yes. It's OK if you win but you're not allowed to have a drink if you lose. He was probably in shock. He couldn't believe it. And he was embarrassed and ashamed about this stupid video, which to me he blew way out of proportion. But he was in this tunnel where he thought he'd messed it all up. So he went into a quick and steep decline."

Simon: "During that period, what could have been done? You said that he was seeking some help. What might have made a difference, do you think?"

Amanda: "He was having therapy sessions. He had 10 sessions. There's obviously the confidentiality but I found out after he made a very serious attempt on his life, when he really hurt himself very badly, that he'd mentioned suicide. I didn't know about that at the time. Of course, I feel that if I'd known, things could have been different. And I did feel that he wasn't really getting better. It was difficult. I felt like maybe he did need more help - maybe residential but we didn't really know where to find that."

Simon: "Debbie, Matt also lost his job..."

Simon: "Were there any signs that he was struggling with mental health, and then was there a steep decline afterwards?"

Debbie: "I think there were changes in behaviour, looking back. Performance-wise the team weren't doing well so there was a lot of abuse on social media. He could never really speak his truth during media interviews of what was going on behind the scenes and he used to sound off to me at home.

"I've found out since that he had spoken to his brother quite a lot about his mental health. But whenever I would say to Matt 'how are things?', he'd be, 'I'm all right, I'm all right', because he always wanted the best for other people.

"He didn't want to concern me and the family that he was having these thoughts and that he was going through these different struggles.

"The sacking came out of the blue and there was a lot of speculation around that. He was starting to drink more than he would have done normally. In terms of his behaviour, I would say he was taking a lot of risks as well. So maybe that was the start of this with him."

Amanda: "Graham was known as a tough competitor. He was a very happy person and loved life, but it can happen to anyone. He wasn't thinking straight really because everything kind of became a vortex. And he just sort of lost the ability to be able to be grounded and think straight. Also you think you're thinking straight when you're not."

Simon: "One of the things about sport that's been discussed is that its reach is enormous. Coaches have a very intimate and closely proximate relationship with people. They can see what's going on with them - even at grassroots level. What would you encourage people to do if they see other people struggling, either in their family or in their community?"

Debbie: "It's a very difficult conversation. It's very hard. But if you're with these people day in, day out, you notice the changes in them. Matt was very intuitive with his players - he could sense things if they weren't playing right. He might have had a conversation with them just one-to-one, away from everyone else, and then make suggestions. There's an awful lot of emphasis on the physical side of someone's wellbeing, but not the mental side. That needs to be explored with people."

Simon: "It's a tough conversation to have, isn't it? Even with your nearest and dearest, let alone with someone on the team. I wonder whether Matt found it difficult when he had to sack players or drop them from the team.

Debbie: "He did. He used to come home and say: 'I've had a hard conversation today with such and such, I've had to let them go and there were tears.' And he'd say: 'I feel guilty.' He was the one who had to deliver the news. He felt tremendous guilt about letting people go."

Simon: "What did Graham's friends in the game come and say to you afterwards? You must have known them - you would have been part of that community."

Amanda: "They were really sad and really gutted. When he was really ill he was ashamed and he shut a lot of people out. So it was hard to get through to him. He would say: 'I've lost all my friends.' And I'm like: 'You haven't.' You know that's his brain. 'You haven't lost your friends at all,' I'd say. But that's how he felt. He felt very isolated."

Simon: "Did Graham have high highs and low lows? I mean, when he scored 100 against Australia or whatever? I just wonder whether he was a person of heightened emotions?"

Amanda: "He always used to say: 'Don't get too down about it... it might not be your day.' And I think if you're going to be like that, then when there are the highs you don't go overboard. He'd say it's his job but it is difficult with people scrutinising what you're doing and everything."

Simon: "What is it that you hope comes out of talking to us and what the Royal Foundation is doing?"

Debbie: "I think with the Royal Foundation, it is exposing the issue and people are going to be talking about it. But there needs to be the right support for when people need it - when they ask for that help.

"It's just making sure that toolkit is followed through and there are people that you can connect with and talk to.

"A connection with a therapist is a difficult one because it's someone you're going to be opening a box to. You want to let everything out but you need to trust that therapist. So it's making sure that there's a good connection there as well - that you feel comfortable talking about your innermost feelings."

Simon: "This is pretty raw for you. Why do you think it's important to talk to the world about this?"

Debbie: "For me and my children, we don't want another family to go through this. It is pretty raw and it's not just the grief, it's the practical side. You've lost a second income. I've still got to pay the same amount of rent, bills, etc. It is the practicality of it and you're juggling all the time - making sure the children are OK... still doing the school runs."

Simon: "You're obviously sad. Are you're angry? Determined?"

Amanda: "I'm angry at myself as well - the guilt you have. 'Why didn't I say that?' And you've got all these 'what ifs'. So all of that nonsense. And, yes - angry as well. 'Couldn't we just have done something?' But, you know, we fall. You know I'm his wife and I still didn't expect that to happen and I ask why he had to go through such a horrible thing. You wouldn't wish it on your worst enemy - and then there's the family as well - my daughters.

"My youngest went off to uni and then Emma went too. So it was just me and the geriatric dog. So it was quite hard."

Debbie: "It's going to be a long road."

Simon: "But it's a road you're both on and I think it's a road you've helped a lot of people with by talking to us."

Debbie: "We've got each other. We've met today and we are going to meet again."

Amanda: "Yes, be a force to be reckoned with! Isn't that what they say?"

Debbie: "Yeah, so I'll come down to you, you come up to me. We're part of this club that we never wanted to be in but we are going to make people listen to what we've got to say. We just want to make a change and help people and just highlight it - we never want anyone else to be in this position. We're going to go great guns aren't we?"

If you are suffering distress or despair, details of help and support are available at BBC Action Line.

title: 'I suffered, but I enjoyed' - Alcaraz on smiling after defeat at 3.34am
description: Carlos Alcaraz discusses his US Open return, why he "misses" rival Jannik Sinner and his excitement for this year's Laver Cup.
fullText:
Most players, after seeing their US Open title defence end at 3.34am after five intense sets, would not walk away smiling.

Carlos Alcaraz is not most players.

After his loss to Ben Shelton - a match that played out over a gruelling four hours and 28 minutes - the Spaniard was filmed walking down the Arthur Ashe tunnel with a huge grin on his face.

Alcaraz had been competing in his first tournament for over five months after suffering a wrist injury that left him in pain every day.

He did not defend his French Open title or compete at Wimbledon, and did not know if he would play in New York until a week before.

"The quarter-final was great - it was a gift for me," Alcaraz told BBC Sport before this week's Laver Cup in London.

"I suffered, but I enjoyed and that's why I smiled when I walked out of the court because I missed that feeling."

The match against Shelton was the latest finish in the tournament's history, and was one of several matches at Flushing Meadows to finish in the early hours.

Eventual champion Alexander Zverev finished past 1am in three of his first five matches, while Venus Williams finished her first-round match at 2am.

"I think it's too much," Alcaraz said of playing so late.

"The last match people stayed but if that match was played earlier, the court could have been packed.

"I would like to change the schedule a little with a maximum finish at 11pm or whatever would be better."

Alcaraz, 23, is one of a number of players to have missed large chunks of the season with injury.

Britain's Jack Draper has had a lengthy struggle with an arm injury, ultimately ending his season early to recover, while Alcaraz's rival Jannik Sinner missed the US Open with a knee injury.

The Spaniard said at the US Open that he will miss some tournaments in the future to allow himself to be "mentally and physically healthy".

He will compete for Team Europe in the Laver Cup at The O2 in London this week, between 25-27 September.

The team tournament pits Europe - captained by Yannick Noah - against a United States team overseen by Andre Agassi.

"When you have your team-mates, the best in the world, by your side, it's a weird feeling but it's beautiful," Alcaraz said.

"We played like our lives depend on it. That's why the Laver Cup is so good to watch as well."

Alcaraz and Italy's Sinner split eight Grand Slam titles between them from 2024 and 2025, establishing a generational rivalry in the process.

They have only met once this year because of injuries, with Sinner winning their sole meeting in the Monte Carlo Masters final to become world number one.

"I have text him not too much, but a few times when he has been winning everything, mostly at the beginning of the year," Alcaraz added.

"I miss him, I miss seeing him around, playing against him. He pushes me to be a better player.

"People will be waiting for those matches, so I think it's going to be better."

title: How the Cubs Playoff Rotation is Shaping Up
description: With the MLB postseason race shaping up, the Chicago Cubs' playoff rotation is becoming clearer. They have occasionally had a rough time with their pitching staff this season, and it has been hard to know who they can trust. However, they are heading for a best-of-three series in the Wild Card round. This means that …
fullText:
With the MLB postseason race shaping up, the Chicago Cubs' playoff rotation is becoming clearer. They have occasionally had a rough time with their pitching staff this season, and it has been hard to know who they can trust. However, they are heading for a best-of-three series in the Wild Card round. This means that they need to start figuring out which three starters make the cut.

Clay Holmes feels safely locked into being one of the three pitchers in the Cubs playoff rotation. Chicago made a massive trade to acquire Holmes at the deadline. Since he returned from injury, it has been worth the cost. He is one of the key players for the Cubs' run in October.

Although his 4.26 ERA is not amazing, it does not tell the full story. He had a strong stretch before struggling in the past three starts, allowing 16 earned runs. This makes it a little concerning, but before that he was rock solid and one of the team's best starters. In four starts before, he allowed only one run. His ability to force ground balls fits in perfectly with the Cubs' elite defense.

Now, the Cubs could play it safe with Holmes and limit his usage over the final week of the regular season. He would be set for one final start, where it may help to play him to get things right. It may be too long of a gap between games, so it would be a surprise if he does not at least pitch a few innings in a game. Before his struggles, it looked like he would be a possible game one starter. Even if he does not get that role, it feels highly unlikely that he does not get a postseason start.

One of the other big trade deadline additions was Kevin Gausman. He is the most experienced pitcher for Chicago, appearing in plenty of postseason games. Since coming to the team, he has given the team good length. Additionally, Chicago has won a majority of his starts.

Heading into his September 23rd start against the Marlins, he has a rough 5.04 ERA with the Cubs. However, like Holmes, that has been inflated by rough games. Gausman is still 4-2 in 44 2/3 innings pitched. His ability to go deep into games is needed with Chicago's rough bullpen. There is a possibility that he is not in the Cubs playoff rotation for the wild card round. Although his experience and durability make it hard not to rely on him.

The third spot is where it gets tricky. Technically, this spot is not guaranteed. If either team wins both of the first two games, the series wouldn't need a third starter. However, if Chicago advanced, the Cubs playoff rotation would be expanded. With this in mind, Matthew Boyd would likely be in the Cubs playoff rotation for the first round.

Boyd has been a reliable option for Chicago this year when he has stayed healthy. He is 9-5 with a 4.06 ERA. The veteran lefty also has plenty of experience at Wrigley Field. If Chicago secures the top Wild Card spot, this would be an advantage. He could very well start either of the first two games as well. The only pitcher possibly above him in the order is Holmes. Boyd and Gausman could come down to which team they face and how they fare against the veteran pitchers.

Shota Imanaga and David Peterson are also hanging around for a possible start. Imanaga is hard to trust with his home run issue, but has seemed to stabilize himself. Peterson is stringing together good starts, and he could very well start in the playoffs. All of the pitchers have question marks around them, but these two may have fewer answers.

When looking at the Cubs playoff rotation, there are multiple ways Chicago can go. All of the starters have shown flashes, but also had very rough games. They still have a week to go, and the decision could be impacted by their opponent. Holmes, Gausman, and Boyd have seemed to separate themselves a bit. Regardless of who gets which game, they will need to set the tone for the series, as it is nearly impossible to trust the bullpen.

title: A Key Safety Feature Shipped in the May OpenTofu Release
description: Dynamic prevent_destroy values make it easier to manage resources like databases with IaC.
fullText:
OpenTofu v1.12.0 was released in May and of the new functionality, there is one that sticks out as worth mentioning: dynamic lifecycle.prevent_destroy.

Before this release, prevent_destroy had to be a static value. Which meant if you wanted destroy protection on your prod instance but not on dev and staging instances of the same root module, you needed to jump through some hoops.

Now prevent_destroy can be defined dynamically so a Multi-Instance root module can do this:

prevent_destroy = var.prevent_destroy_enabled

Your prod root module instance can now set prevent_destroy_enabled = true. Dev and ephemeral instances can default it to false and tear down freely without intervention.

This is a UX improvement I love to see because it makes safety easy. Particularly when we've seen big clients who manage lots of databases be spooked by managing DBs via IaC (suffering from fear of resource deletion), this feels like it'll calm nerves and help adoption (even if only slightly).

Also worth a look in this release: the new destroy = false lifecycle option, which removes a resource from state without destroying the real infrastructure. Another nice safety lever for day-2 ops!

The OpenTofu team keeps shipping and I'm a fan!

title: Australia says OpenAI agent hacked into government website
description: The OpenAI agent gained unauthorised access to public and non-public files in what could be the first known instance of an AI agent hacking a government website.
fullText:
The OpenAI agent gained unauthorised access to public and non-public files in what could be the first known instance of an AI agent hacking a government website.

SYDNEY: Australia said on Wednesday (Sep 23) an OpenAI agent breached a government health data portal in June, gaining unauthorised access to files, in what could be the first known instance of an AI agent hacking a government website.

The breach is one of the highest-profile incidents of AI agents accessing external systems outside the United States, coming on top of several recent breaches globally by rogue AI agents that have alarmed governments and companies.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the OpenAI agent gained unauthorised access to the medical statistics portal of a government agency responsible for non-sensitive health data and statistics, including public medical spending.

"Evidence currently available is there is no broader compromise to the ... network. Nonetheless, this situation is obviously unacceptable," Albanese said during a media briefing in New York, where he is attending the UN General Assembly.

Investigations continue and Australia had voiced its "extreme concern about this incident" to OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Albanese said, adding that he was deeply disappointed by the company's delay in notifying the government.

"It took until Sep 10 before there was any notification at all," Albanese said, adding that the investigation would also examine why government systems had failed to detect the breach in the first place.

He also warned that three other government websites "may be impacted" by the OpenAI agent's activity.

"The question is, when it was trying to harvest data, did it go into these other sites? So we're not confirming that that occurred," he said.

The incident comes after OpenAI and Anthropic, in separate submissions to a parliamentary inquiry this month, urged Australia to reconsider a ban preventing them from using the country's creative content to train their models.

"Our review found no evidence of patient records being accessed. The information accessed included aggregate health statistics and internal file names," OpenAI said in a statement.

It added that it "identified activity involving several Australian government websites and services as our models attempted to look up answers ... our models took actions we did not intend".The breach is one of several recent incidents in which OpenAI has disclosed hacks or unauthorised activity involving its AI agents well after they occurred.

In some cases this was because the activity was only detected belatedly, and in others because the company initially elected not to disclose it.

A separate high-profile incident, a mid-July intrusion into open-source AI repository Hugging Face, was only detected about a week after it took place, according to timelines released by OpenAI and independent investigators.

This helped ignite a global conversation about the risks posed by increasingly powerful AI models.

Rivals Anthropic, Google's Gemini, and Meta have also disclosed incidents of their agents accessing external systems.

Some of America's top AI executives, including Altman, have called for a slowdown of AI development, citing, among other things, the threat of devastating cyberattacks by out-of-control agents.
