fullText:
The new wearables come at a time of uncertainty for smart glasses, which are facing backlash over privacy concerns

Meta announced an advanced new set of virtual reality glasses and a collection of new smart glasses Wednesday, including an audio-only version without a camera.

At the firm’s Meta Connect conference in Menlo Park, California, executives said the new Ray-Ban Meta models set new standards for battery life and weight. They said the new glasses with screens in the lenses squeeze capabilities previously reserved for a full headset into a light set of spectacles that rest on a user’s ears.

The new wearables come at a time of uncertainty for the smart glasses category, which is broadly facing a backlash from sceptics and privacy campaigners around their ability to record video, frequently being dubbed “perv glasses” or “spy glasses”. Meta’s smart glasses are the most popular gadget in the category.

The Ray-Ban Meta Audio AI glasses seem tailored for the time. Lacking a camera, they may help avert some privacy worries, though Meta claims they have been in the works for several years. The glasses have microphones and speakers for music, calls and interacting with the company’s AI assistant, taking the recognizable form of Ray Ban’s Clubmaster or Burbank styles. The new versions are thinner and lighter than the camera versions and last up to 12 hours on battery and will cost £319 (€349/A$529).

The new Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 glasses, which do sport cameras, have longer battery life than their predecessors, lasting up to nine hours with support for Dolby Atmos audio. They will cost £409 (€449/A$679). Meta is also launching two new styles of its own-brand glasses in partnership with singer and actor Lisa. All of the firm’s smart glasses have an LED warning light that flashes when recording, but Meta said it has made improvements to its tampering detection, including during a livestream.

Finally, Meta is expanding availability of its Meta Ray-Ban Display smart glasses to outside the US for the first time since their announcement a year ago. The glasses with a virtual display in the right lens will go on sale in the UK and Canada from 23 September priced at £749 (CA$1,149) and will later expand to France, Germany and Italy on 13 October for €899.

The new Meta VR glasses are an evolution of the company’s pioneering Quest VR headsets, which have become some of the most popular on the market. But instead of being a bulky plastic headset, the 100g device is made of magnesium alloy and looks like an oversized set of glasses. The wearer peers through small lenses on to a 5K microOLED screen with a crisp 37 pixels per degree, making text look sharp and rivalling Apple’s high-end Vision Pro headset. Users can see out of the sides and through a camera system at the front for augmented reality features and awareness of their surroundings.

The glasses are tethered by a cable to a pocketable 300g puck containing the computing power and three-hour battery pack, which helps to remove the weight from a user’s head and makes the glasses five times lighter than the Quest 3 headsets, according to Meta.

The glasses are fully compatible with the vast Quest software library, but are designed for productivity and entertainment rather than games. The company described the glasses as “IMAX Enhanced” and supportive of 3D for movies. At launch, they will showcase a new Disney+ immersive experience that reflects landscapes from films such as Avengers: Infinity War surrounding a virtual cinema screen.

The glasses have the ability to display multiple virtual windows and to connect to a Mac or PC to mirror its displays. They have eye-tracking and hand-gesture control, including a virtual keyboard projected on to any desk or table, but also support Quest’s hand controllers or an Xbox game pad for games.

The Meta VR glasses will cost $1,299.99 and will be available from spring 2027 in North America, Europe and Asia.

title: Albanese says OpenAI hacked Medicare and told Australia months later via email to generic inbox
description:
Prime minister says he told Sam Altman he was disappointed it had taken OpenAI ‘way too long’ to disclose breach
Anthony Albanese says an artificial intelligence agent developed by OpenAI hacked Medicare in June and the tech giant notified the government earlier this month using an email sent to a “public mailbox”.
Australia’s prime minister made the comments at the UN summit in New York, saying it appeared no personal information had been accessed in the AI breach.
 Continue reading...
fullText:
Prime minister says he told Sam Altman he was disappointed it had taken OpenAI ‘way too long’ to disclose breach

Anthony Albanese says an artificial intelligence agent developed by OpenAI hacked Medicare in June and the tech giant notified the government earlier this month using an email sent to a “public mailbox”.

Australia’s prime minister made the comments at the UN summit in New York, saying it appeared no personal information had been accessed in the AI breach.

Investigations assisted by the Australian Signals Directorate were ongoing into how the agent had infiltrated Australia’s government-run universal health care system, as well as three others.

They were the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, the Victorian Department of Health, the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, and the Medicare Statistics Reporting Service Portal of Services Australia.

“This situation is obviously unacceptable,” Albanese said.

“Today, I spoke with the CEO of OpenAI, Sam Altman, to express Australia’s extreme concern about this incident and I also expressed my disappointment that it took the company way too long to inform the government what had occurred.”

Albanese said both the delay and the manner in which OpenAI notified the government was disappointing.

“It took until 10 September before there was any notification at all. And the notification was an email sent to just the public mailbox,” Albanese said.

The email was sent to the public-facing email address publicdisclosures@servicesaustralia.gov.au . That inbox is checked once a day: the email was not read until 11 September.

Services Australia then reported the notification to the Australian Cyber Security Centre on 15 September.

A taskforce has been launched to explore the “legal situation” of the breach.

On Thursday, the NSW premier Chris Minns and the Victorian premier Ben Carroll both said Albanese had informed them the OpenAI breach had affected state websites – NSW’s crime agency and Victoria’s health department.

Both Minns and Carroll said it did not appear any personal information had been shared in the breach, though investigations were ongoing.

“New South Wales will be working with commonwealth intelligence agencies to get to the bottom of it,” Minns said.

Albanese said the OpenAI agent had gained unauthorised access into the public-facing Medicare statistics reporting service portal, which is administered by Services Australia.

The portal contains non-sensitive Medicare information relating to data and statistics, such as spending.

Albanese said the agent had accessed “public and non-public files within the portal” and, in order to do this, “engaged in writing files as well to the internal server”.

The deputy prime minister, Richard Marles, said the government learned of the June breach “a couple of weeks ago” and ministers were informed last week.

Marles said the agent was non-human and he called the breach a “very serious incident”.

“What we have seen is unauthorised access in to an Australian government website and that is completely unacceptable and we have made that clear to OpenAI,” he said.

The AI agent had been given “a benign task” of researching health and medical statistics and, in doing so, had approached, as well as the Medicare portal, the three other Australian websites.

“In relation to those three, it interacted in a way that a member of the public might, so it only acted in an authorised way,” Marles told ABC radio on Thursday.

“But in relation to the medical portal of Services Australia, it sought information, information was not given, and then it effectively hacked into that medical portal and got that information anyway.

“It’s that unauthorised access which we are very concerned about. The impact is relatively minor, but the incident is very serious.”

Marles said the government had established a taskforce led by the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet that was working with the Australian Signals Directorate and the AI Safety Institute.

“We will look at what is the legal situation in respect of this and what it means to have gained an unauthorised access, albeit in an unintended way,” the acting prime minister said.

“This is a warning about the fact that artificial intelligence, which is a technology that has huge opportunity to benefit humanity, has to be developed with enormous care. There have to be guardrails and safety measures in place which are way ahead of the capability which is being developed.”

The OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company was conducting an extensive review of “misaligned model activity during training and evaluation” and was “notifying third parties when our review identifies potential impacts to their systems”.

“During this review, we identified activity involving several Australian government websites and services as our models attempted to look up answers, and available statistics for questions about Australia during an internal evaluation,” Pusateri said in a statement.

“In the course of that, our models took actions we did not intend.”

He said the review had found aggregate health statistics and internal file names had been accessed but there was “no evidence of patient records being accessed”.

Pusateri said OpenAI was supporting investigations and that its review was ongoing, adding it was committed “sharing what we learn as that work continues”.

Lizzie O’Shea, spokesperson for Digital Rights Watch, said the fact it took three months for OpenAI to tell the government showed that there needed to be “basic rules and standards for tech companies”.

“Artificial intelligence has potential to do some things well, but it also poses huge risks – like hacking systems that store Australians’ sensitive personal data,” O’Shea said on Thursday.

“The question is whether governments are going to let AI and tech companies run wild or whether they, on behalf of ordinary people, will put rules in place for tech companies that will promote accountability and trust.”

Independent senator David Pocock said the OpenAI hack highlighted how slow the government had been to implement AI safeguards in high-risk settings.

Pocock criticised the government’s decision to shelve plans for a National AI Safety Act, and its dilatory approach to legislating new standards.

“We have these companies warning of existential threat and hacking critical government infrastructure and the Labor government’s response is ‘We’ll get to that next year’.

“There is also a big question here around why we aren’t holding these big tech companies liable for this kind of data breach. If it was an Australian who hacked the system they’d likely be heading for jail, yet there’s no accountability for AI companies developing this technology.”

Ed Santo, former human rights commissioner and co-founder of the Human Technology Institute, told ABC radio that Australians ought to “be worried”.

“This is the first time that this has happened in any major way to an Australian database, and it’s one of the most sensitive databases that we have in government.”

OpenAI had “instructed their AI agents to go looking for information about the public health system in Australia. When the AI agents couldn’t easily find that information, they decided to break the law,” Santo said.

Describing the behaviour as “misaligned model activity” was using “a very euphemistic term”, he said.

“If we were in the bricks and mortar world, if an employee of a company went and broke the law, particularly if it broke the criminal law, then that individual would suffer serious legal consequences, but so would their company. And so we need to make sure that that is true also in this era of AI.”

title: How Garmin's New 'Epic' Feature Helps Me See the Bigger Picture of My Training
description: Garmin Epics are more useful than meets the eye.
fullText:
Garmin's new logging feature, Garmin Epic, is getting buried in the launch of the latest Fenix 9 watch, but it deserves a headline of its own. It's a shareable digital travel journal for your big trip, being pitched by Garmin as the kind of thing you post after a major hike or race. Personally, I think that framing undersells it. Epic is also a great training-analysis hack, and that's how I plan on using it for my upcoming marathon this fall.

First things first: Garmin Epics are not to be confused with Garmin's older watch line, epix, with an "x". This feature is Epic, with a "c". The names are close enough that searching for one turns up the other, so double-check the spelling.

A Garmin Epic is a digital travel journal that combines your activities, maps, photos, and key health and performance metrics into a single interactive timeline you can revisit and share. With the Fenix 9 smartwatch, you can create and start an Epic directly from your watch. For older watches, you can still create Epics in the Garmin Connect app.

Once you create an Epic, you can see all activities on one map, photos, an activity feed, daily notes, and selected performance and health reports across the whole span. It's a free Garmin Connect feature, and Garmin's launch demo showed a Reports tab with sleep score, resting heart rate, and HRV status for the same dates.

Again, although the launch of Garmin Epic is wrapped up in the launch of the Fenix 9, you don't need that smartwatch to use Epics in the Connect app: You can find it under the Activities menu. You can also group past activities into an Epic after the fact, and that ability is what makes the training-hack angle work.

An Epic can run up to 92 days and keeps cumulative distance and calories along with sleep, recovery, and HRV status. That's about 13 weeks, which conveniently covers a typical training block for a half-marathon-level event. Here are some ways to use it:

Wrap a whole training block. Make one Epic per build, such as "Fall Marathon Build" or "Base Phase." You get total volume and the recovery trend in a single view, and you can compare it against your next block.

Review a training camp or big week. Garmin lists training camps as a use case: Group the days, see total volume, and check how fitness and recovery responded over time.

Look back at a build after the race. Backdate an Epic across the last 10 weeks and see whether your HRV status and sleep held up. Then you can decide what to repeat for next time.

Track a return from injury or a taper. Sometimes these are periods where the trend matters more than any single run.

Use daily notes as a subjective log. "Legs heavy," "slept badly," "felt great." The metrics show what your body did, but your notes show how it felt, which is usually what explains a strange week.

Plan ahead. You can schedule up to five future Epics, up to 366 days in advance. Set up your next block before it starts.

Garmin Epic wasn't designed to be a comprehensive training-analysis feature, so it's not a flawless system. Still, while Epic is marketed as the place to relive your adventures, I'd argue the more useful trick is using it to zoom out and look for patterns in your training for next time.

title: Apple Has a Fix for Your New Apple Watch's Restart Bug
description: If you bought an Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4, you'll want to update ASAP.
fullText:
Apple's latest Apple Watches, the Series 12 and the Ultra 4, should be the "best" smartwatches the company has to offer. While they're minor upgrades over the Series 11 and Ultra 3, there are some key improvements, including the new S11 chip and a heart rate monitor that checks your pulse every five seconds. If you picked up one of these watches, you might have put these new upgrades to the test—that is, if your watch didn't restart on you.

As reported by MacRumors, Apple's latest smartwatches appear prone to unexpected restarts. That's according to numerous posts on the site's forums, with users saying their watches abruptly show a blank screen with the Apple logo. There doesn't appear to be any particular action that triggers it: Users say their watches rebooted when recording a workout, using Siri AI, editing watch faces, or using the Maps app. Many users on this Reddit thread share similar experiences with their new watches. Some users dug deeper, pulling their Apple Watches' diagnostics at the time of rebooting. Rather than a specific function, the culprit appears to be a timeout with the Neural Engine, the hardware that processes Apple's AI features.

Users tried multiple workarounds themselves: One Redditor simply turned the watch off and on themself, and the issue never returned; others tried resetting the watch as new, but experienced rebooting again. MacRumors highlighted one case where a user received a replacement from Apple, and it, too, rebooted unexpectedly. It does appear to be an issue with the Series 12 and Ultra 4, and, luckily, Apple figured it out.

On Wednesday, Apple unexpectedly released watchOS 27.0.1. The update has a brief changelog, with only one new addition: "This update provides bug fixes for your Apple Watch, including fixing an issue where Apple Watch may restart unexpectedly." Apple didn't clarify exactly what it changed to fix the issue, but at least the reboots should be over.

This update is only for Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 users, so don't expect to see it unless you have one of Apple's newest wearables. If you do, make sure to install it as soon as possible to avoid dealing with these unexpected restarts. To install watchOS 27.0.1, head to the Apple Watch app, then tap My Watch and go to General > Software Update.

title: I Tried Siri AI on My New Apple Watch, and I'm Frustrated
description: When it works, it's great—but it rarely works smoothly.
fullText:
One of the big features Apple announced alongside the new Apple Watches is Siri AI—now available on your wrist! You need to join a waitlist to try Apple's new and improved chatbot, and since my turn just came up, I put the new on-wrist Siri through its paces. Here's how it went, and why I don't think the experience lives up to Apple's promises (yet, anyway).

Since Siri AI requires Apple Intelligence, you’ll need a device that supports it. Those include iPhones 15 Pro and newer, and an Apple Watch that is Series 9 or newer. If you want to use Siri AI on the Apple Watch, you need both a supported watch and a supported phone—a new watch and old phone won’t do the trick. With my phone and watch both on iOS 27 (the iOS 27.2 developer beta on the phone; watchOS 27.0 on the Apple Watch Series 12), I enabled Siri AI in my phone’s Settings app, which put me on a waiting list. A few days later, I got a notification that I was in.

Once I'd upgraded to Siri AI on my watch, I went about asking it plenty of questions and watched it struggle to answer many of them. The first thing I tried was to ask where I could find the nearest yoga studio; it responded with a list of yoga studios, none of them particularly close to my home. After rewording my question a few times, it finally listed one about a mile away. This is one of those examples where using AI is less efficient than a Google search—or even plain old regular Siri: When I asked this same question of the old Siri model last week, it quickly found the closest studio.

With my phone in another room, I next decided to try some of the questions that Apple provides as examples on the WatchOS 27 page. Here’s how that went.

“What’s a good warm-up for deadlifts?” Siri gave me paragraphs of text about the purpose of warmups in general. When I tapped "Show More," I was sent to the bottom of a long bulleted list of exercises. I’m not reading all that.

“Read my upcoming events.” Siri needed a good five seconds to think about this one, but then correctly rattled off my next few calendar appointments.

“Set a new move ring goal.” Actually, I first started by asking what my Move ring goal was, and Siri could not tell me. So I blindly set a new goal, and later saw it updated to the new value in the Fitness app...sort of. When I asked for a goal of burning 350 calories, it gave me a goal of 350. When I asked for a goal of 325, Siri responded that it has changed my goal to 325, but when I checked the Fitness app, it showed that my goal had been set to 320 calories.

I then put Siri AI to the test with a few requests that other Apple Watch users have reported give the chatbot some trouble. The first involved setting a timer; perhaps that function is buggy for some users, but it worked quickly for me. “Siri, set a timer for five minutes” did exactly that, with only a few seconds of waiting. Likewise, “Siri, what’s the weather for today?” brought up the weather forecast instantly.

One of the purported new features of Siri AI is its ability to search your emails and messages for information that is relavent to a conversation you're having with it. On the Apple Watch, this doesn’t work for me as well as I would like. First, I asked Siri what my daughter had recently asked me to buy for her. (She is constantly texting me to ask for things.) Siri responded that my daughter had sent me a wish list of LEGO sets on Sept. 12. This is true. But it wasn’t until I specified, “wasn’t there a makeup kit?” that Siri was also able to find that request, which was from Sept. 13.

Meanwhile, the iPhone version of Siri AI was able to find the wishlist and makeup kit requests and tell me about them in the same initial response, without the additional prompting. In another test of its search capabilities, I asked who I had sent “Ramona’s dad’s phone number” to. The Watch version of Siri AI found that text message, but was only able to tell me the phone number of the person I had sent it to. Siri AI on the phone, on the other hand, was able to figure out that the person requesting the number had introduced themselves by name earlier in that conversation, and it told me exactly who that person was (even though I had not entered the name into my contacts).

Still, plenty of requests don’t work even that well, or don’t work at all. The watch’s Siri app routinely crashes, taking me back to the home screen. Sometimes Siri’s voice breaks up, and it interrupts itself to start its message over again. Good save, but weird to listen to. Sometimes Siri “thinks” for a long time. Many requests take five to 10 seconds, during which time I certainly could grab my phone and look up the answer myself. Whenever Siri is stumped, it searches the web and gives me a sea of unhelpful text.

For example, I tried to see if Siri could explain a mysterious icon on my watch screen. I asked, “Why is this icon gray?” (in a variety of phrasings to clarify I meant one that I was looking at right now). Instead of telling me anything useful, or explaining that it can't see my watch screen, it read me some text from the Internet about what gray icons mean, in general, as a concept. Another time, I asked it to resume playing my podcast. Instead of starting up my usual podcast app, it told me that Episode 550 of My Favorite Murder had just come out. I don’t like murder podcasts, have never listened to My Favorite Murder in my life, and episode 550 was—now that I check—the third-most-recent episode, not the one that just came out. (The iPhone’s version of Siri AI, on the other hand, happily started my podcast app.)

At least one thing worked better on the watch: Both versions of Siri AI said they had no information on my sleep data, but the version on the watch was at least able to tell me what time I had gone to bed and what time I had woken up. That's something.

The promised Conversations app likewise did not work as expected. When you press the digital crown on the watch, a mini app picker pops up with Siri in the center, surrounded by a few of your most recent apps. If you scroll down, you get the full list (or grid) as before. Tapping that center button is supposed to show you a list of recent conversations, but mine kept showing me “No conversations.” Later, exactly one conversation showed up there: the one where I asked what a gray icon meant. That was the only question in that conversation, even though I had been conversing with Siri all day.

I like the idea of the new Siri AI, and being able to ask follow-up questions is nice, especially now that I can interrupt the chatbot to clarify my questions. (“Give me two specific warm-up exercises I can do before snatches” got it to stop lecturing me about warm-ups in general.) But the long waits for answers, the frequent crashes, and the bot's inability to access data that is right there on the device are frustrating. Here’s hoping it gets better with the next update.

title: Burnham says ban on alcohol for football fans in stands is 'discrimination'
description: The prime minister opposes the law - in place since 1985 - and believes there is a case to remove it.
fullText:
Andy Burnham has branded a ban on fans being allowed to drink alcohol in the stands during men's football matches as "discrimination".

The prime minister told reporters that "I don't think it's fair for football fans to be singled out", as he suggested a change could be trialled.

Laws are in place which prevent drinking in view of the pitch at stadiums for clubs in the top five tiers of men's football in England. Other sports do not face such a restriction.

The Football Supporters' Association (FSA) said the "outdated" legislation should be reviewed, but police chiefs have warned against relaxing the law and would like to meet the PM to "explain the challenges".

The legislation was introduced in 1985 by Margaret Thatcher's government for English and Welsh football grounds. At the time, then-Home Secretary Leon Brittan said that alcohol was a "major contributory factor in violent and disorderly behaviour" in football grounds.

Burnham is a keen football fan and a season-ticket holder at Premier League team Everton.

Shortly before he became prime minister, he criticised the restriction on football fans as he attended a rugby league game at Everton's Hill Dickinson Stadium where it was possible for supporters to have a drink in the stands.

Speaking to reporters on his trip to the United Nations in New York, Burnham was asked if it was still his view now he is in Downing Street.

Burnham replied: "I think that legislation dates to an era where football was very different.

"And I do believe there is a case to remove that discrimination. There are different ways it could be done. It could happen on a trial basis.

"But I'm not going to back away from what's been a long held view of mine. I don't see how it can be fair that some supporters of one sport can be treated differently."

Government sources have stressed that Burnham was restating an opinion that he has long held, rather than making any sort of policy announcement.

The prime minister's comments are not being seen inside government as an indication that he is looking to change the law in the area.

A trial or pilot scheme to look at whether a change would be possible is not being ruled out but any wider move would require extensive consultation involving football clubs, fans and the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport - none of which is currently planned.

A UK Football Policing Unit (UKFPU) spokesman warned that changes to the law would pose "challenges" to policing and the "safety of staff and fans at football games".

He said: "Other sports simply don't see the violence and criminal behaviour from their supporters that football does, albeit a minority, with alcohol often playing a significant part in violent and disorderly behaviour.

"It would be irresponsible to fuel this by allowing greater alcohol consumption during games."

He added it would be "incredibly rash to make fundamental changes without a full examination of the evidence and meaningful consultation with police practitioners who have the expertise in this area".

FSA chairman Tom Greatrex said it was "unfair to criminalise football fans for having a pint while watching the match - especially since you can sit in the same seat drinking alcohol whilst watching an Oasis gig or rugby league".

He said "many clubs" were in favour of a change, adding: "We welcome the prime minister's comments and totally agree that the legislation is outdated and deserves to be reviewed."

A fan-led review of football governance in 2021 called for the law to be re-examined.

The rules have been relaxed this season with all Women's Super League (WSL) clubs allowed to offer alcohol to supporters in the stands following two seasons of successful trials.

The law is more restrictive in Scotland, where the general sale of alcohol has been prohibited in Scottish football stadiums since 1981, but trial sales have been taking place recently and fans can now buy alcohol at Hampden Park games.

title: Spotlight on new coaches as road to Afcon 2027 begins
description: Patrick Vieira and Herve Renard are among the high-profile managerial arrivals as the qualification campaign for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations gets under way.
fullText:
Just eight months on from the final of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) - and with the world still waiting to find out the ultimate destination of the title - the road to the 2027 tournament begins in earnest.

The 48 sides still in contention will play two rounds of qualifying in this extended international window, which gets under way on Thursday.

Two more matches follow in November, with the groups reaching their denouement with the final two fixtures in March.

The top two in nine of the 12 groups will progress to the 24-team finals in Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda.

Preparations for the tournament in East Africa may be lagging behind but, with the three hosts all guaranteed qualification, there is only one spot on offer in their respective groups. That means a second-placed finish may potentially not be enough.

Several managerial changes have occurred since the last Afcon in Morocco and this year's Fifa World Cup, while several star players have hung up their boots. Here's what to keep an eye on in the first two rounds of action.

Senegal appeal date set after Afcon win overturned

Among several coaching changes, two in particular have caught the eye.

Herve Renard, the only man to win Afcon with two different nations, has returned to the Ivory Coast job some 11 years after leading the West Africans to the title.

The 57-year-old Frenchman starts his second stint with the Elephants at home against Ghana on Thursday in what is the standout match in the first round of fixtures.

In the opposing dugout, the experienced Carlos Queiroz is back at the helm after leading the Black Stars to the last 32 at the World Cup. However, Tottenham's Mohammed Kudus is among a number of players to withdraw from his squad.

Patrick Vieira is another high-profile arrival, as the 1998 World Cup champion with France takes charge of Senegal, the country of his birth.

The former Arsenal midfielder, 50, describes the role as "an absolute dream" yet he will begin with two away games against Mozambique and Ethiopia because Dakar is getting ready to host the 2026 Youth Olympics.

Africa prepares for historic Olympic moment at Dakar 2026

Cape Verde were one of the great stories of the 2026 World Cup, pushing Argentina all the way in the last 32 before the debutants lost 3-2 after extra time.

Long-serving coach Bubista has since resigned from the Blue Sharks hotseat, with his former assistant Humberto Bettencourt stepping up.

He will begin his reign in Mali on Friday before hosting Rwanda on Tuesday.

Algeria, Tunisia and South Africa have also changed coaches since the World Cup.

The Tunisians have turned to former Esperance and Renaissance Berkane boss Moin Chaaban as they aim to move on from their disastrous World Cup campaign which saw Sabri Lamouchi dismissed after one game and Renard fail to orchestrate a revival.

Pitso Mosimane has been reappointed by South Africa some 14 years on from his last spell in charge - which saw Bafana Bafana miss out on the 2012 Afcon - and Brahim Hemdani has taken over Algeria after Vladmir Petkovic's departure.

Meanwhile, Afcon legend Claude Le Roy has returned at the age of 78 after signing on for a second stint with Congo-Brazzaville.

The Red Devils have not appeared at the finals since 2015, while Frenchman Le Roy is aiming to coach at a record-extending 10th edition of the finals.

Burkina Faso have turned to ex-Comoros boss Amir Abdou and, after a stint with Libya, 2021 Afcon-winning coach Aliou Cisse has his first competitive matches in charge of Angola.

The former Senegal boss starts with a tough away assignment in Egypt.

Some big-name players have called time on their international careers since the World Cup, with several of them former Afcon winners.

Senegal are looking for a new number one after Edouard Mendy hung up his goalkeeping gloves.

The 34-year-old helped the Teranga Lions become champions at the 2021 and 2025 tournaments - even if the latter title is still disputed at the Court of Arbitration for Sport.

Wing wizard Riyad Mahrez, who captained Algeria to the trophy in 2019, has quit international duty while Ivory Coast will have to cope without midfielders Seko Fofana and Jean-Michael Seri.

Ellyes Skhiri has also called time on his international career and will not be involved as Tunisia aim to reach a record-extending 18th consecutive Afcon.

Meanwhile, Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang has stepped back from Gabon duty, saying he felt "humiliated" by his treatment after their exit at the previous tournament.

The 37-year-old was excluded from the national team set-up after their group-stage exit. That sanction was later lifted, but Aubameyang ruled himself out of Sebastien Migne's Panthers squad despite his fine start to the season with Deportivo La Coruna.

Elsewhere, Eritrea are back in the group stage of Afcon qualifiers - for the first time since the build-up to the 2008 edition - after seeing off Eswatini 4-1 on aggregate in the preliminary round in March.

Chad, Djibouti, Mauritius, Sao Tome and Principe and Seychelles are the other five nations already eliminated.

However, seven Ertirea players absconded after the away leg of their tie which was held in South Africa.

Occurrences of Eritrean sportsmen and women failing to return home to what is a one-party state and a highly militarised society has long been an issue, and was part of the reason for the East Africans withdrawing from qualifying for both the 2023 Afcon and 2026 World Cup.

Yet the Red Sea Camels, who have been drawn alongside Kenya, South Africa and Guinea in Group D, are now largely relying on talent drawn from the diaspora.

Just three home-based players have been named in the squad for their opening two fixtures, which see them take on the tournament co-hosts in Nairobi on Saturday before a 'home' game against Bafana Bafana in Cairo on Tuesday.

Meanwhile, Somalia have reached the group stage of qualifying for the first ever time but face a very tricky draw alongside Ivory Coast, Ghana and The Gambia.

The Ocean Stars are ranked 53rd on the continent but, like Eritrea, can at least dream of reaching Afcon as the tournament returns to East Africa for the first time since 1976.

title: When Bellamy watched on as Ronaldo caused lockdown
description: Craig Bellamy says Cristiano Ronaldo is "beyond a superstar" before his Wales side face the Portugal legend in the opening match of their Nations League A campaign.
fullText:
With five Ballon d'Or wins, eight league titles, five Champions Leagues, a European Championship and a pair of Nations League triumphs among his glut of honours, Cristiano Ronaldo's status as one of football's all-time greats is not in doubt.

But a chance encounter with the Portugal legend helped Wales boss Craig Bellamy appreciate that the 41-year-old is significantly more than just a footballing icon.

Bellamy was on a pre-season trip to Lisbon during his time as an assistant to manager Vincent Kompany at Burnley when the Portuguese capital's airport was effectively put into lockdown.

It led to the Welshman describing Ronaldo as "beyond a superstar" after he realised the vast presence of police and security officials were to help escort the global icon.

"So we got to the airport and the police were everywhere. It was on lockdown," Bellamy said.

Ronaldo spurred on by 1,000 goals and Portugal glory

Live on BBC iPlayer, BBC One Wales, BBC Sounds, BBC Radio Wales, Radio Cymru and 5 Live, BBC Sport website and app, plus live text commentary.

"We're Burnley and we had a little bit of VIP. We were on a coach, we were chartered but still had to go into the airport a certain way.

"It was like rows of police with police cars everywhere. We thought, 'something has happened, there must be a warning here'.

"Everything was locked off. People in the terminal, you name it. We couldn't get off the coach and we had to wait for what we thought was a security breach or something.

"We are stuck on the coach for 10, 15 minutes and suddenly this car turns up, it parks and a guy walks out, goes in the boot, grabs a rucksack and someone else gets out and puts the rucksack on and who is it? Ronaldo."

Bellamy added: "He is walking on his own with police everywhere and Lisbon airport locked off. Even the police were taking pictures. No-one could bother him.

"It was the coolest walk I have ever watched for a minute.

"We were all on the coach and our jaws dropped. Everyone who had been moaning quickly shut up. It was like presidents stuff."

Bellamy last shared a pitch with Ronaldo in October 2008 as the Portuguese scored twice for Manchester United in a 2-0 Premier League win over West Ham United at Old Trafford.

He is now set to manage his country against the 233-cap international as Wales kick-start their Nations League A campaign in Portugal on Thursday night.

As he bids to conjure up a plan to nullify Ronaldo and the rest of the star-studded Portugal squad at the Estadio Jose Alvalade, Bellamy was eager to fully reflect on the experience of the forward he witnessed at Lisbon airport.

"How can you lock off a whole airport?" added Bellamy.

"I would not be able to get my computer through customs in Cardiff airport. What have I just seen?

"The reason I'm telling the story is because that's how big this guy is.

"It was like, 'wow'. I'm so glad I saw that moment because he is beyond a superstar."

What will 'greatest captain' bring to Bellamy's Wales?

FAW chief questions Infantino's Fifa reform claims

During the summer, Ronaldo confirmed the 2026 World Cup would be his last.

However, the Al-Nassr frontman has so far not revealed when he will finally bring his glittering career to an end.

Despite the uncertainty surrounding Ronaldo's future, Bellamy says he can fully understand why the forward - now in his 24th year as a senior Portugal international - is still operating at an elite level.

"I'm not surprised he is still playing with the professionalism he has shown," added Bellamy.

"It's also how clever he is, he knows how to protect himself, he knows not to waste his energy at certain times and he's still got the habit of goal-scoring, and you never lose that.

"We're talking about not just one of the greatest players of our generation, we're talking all generations with what he has been able to do. He's beyond a superstar."

Inside the Wales camp: Jordan James & Connor Roberts

For all of the spotlight on Ronaldo and his team-mates, Bellamy knows his full focus - along with that of his players and staff - must be on how Wales can leave the City of Light with a positive result.

The head coach's already tough task has been made harder by the fact he will be without players including Harry Wilson, Joe Rodon, Karl Darlow, Nathan Broadhead, Dylan Lawlor, Rubin Colwill and Isaak Davies in Lisbon.

But Bellamy has urged his players to show the right kind of fight as they bid to upset the odds and remain in the top tier of the Nations League over the coming months.

"We have to be excited, but not too excited," he added.

"We have worked hard to get into League A, so what can we do to stay in it? If we do then it will help us massively and that's the motivation.

"You want to be in these moments. I'm telling you, when your playing days finish, you won't remember Bury away and all that. These moments you will remember and will live with you.

"But you also want to remember how you performed. You don't want this to get too much.

"I want my players to go out and give everything. They should love every second of it. That's the drive for this."

fullText:
WASHINGTON – Maine Sen. Susan Collins' Republican colleagues swiftly came to her defense the day after the news outlet ProPublica published an investigative story that laid out evidence of alleged involvement in a pay-to-play scheme involving a defense contractor.

The story, which came out on Tuesday, Sept. 22, said that records and emails showed the FBI sought to launch a sweeping investigation examining Collins' interactions with a top donor who won lucrative federal contracts. By late 2024, the agency reportedly had enough evidence to pursue a sweeping bribery probe involving Collins and other members of Congress.

But that effort, according to the ProPublica story, evaporated after the Trump administration purged the Justice Department and FBI of its teams that handle public corruption cases.

It's unclear whether the accusations laid out in the article will resonate with Maine voters in November, when Collins is up for reelection in a toss-up race that will prove crucial to whichever party ultimately controls the Senate.

The story does, however, add to a maze of obstacles she's facing to retain her coveted seat in Congress. While she has a track record as a Teflon political candidate in the Pine Tree State, her campaign is already being hurt by an unpopular war, President Trump's trade disputes with Canada and the sudden departure of her initial, scandal-plagued opponent.

Both Collins and her top spokespeople denied any impropriety following the publication of the ProPublica article, saying the Justice Department, dating back to the Biden administration, cleared the senator and her staff of any alleged wrongdoing.

Collins told a Wall Street Journal opinion columnist she was the victim of a "partisan hit job" and questioned why anyone would "take the word of a convicted felon," referring to the defense contractor at the center of the scandal whose cooperation was relied on by investigators to build their case.

"It is so offensive," she said. "This is a smear job."

Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, told USA TODAY the accusations were a "bunch of BS." Asked why he thought so, he said, "because I know Susan Collins." Cornyn and Collins have served together in the Senate for more than two decades.

Sen. Katie Britt, R-Alabama, who sits on the powerful Senate Appropriations Committee which Collins leads, argued her Maine colleague has the "utmost ethical standards."

"I have zero concern for any kind of baseless accusations," she told USA TODAY.

Perhaps Collins' quickest – and most politically important – defender was Senate Majority Leader John Thune.

"I don't think there's ever been any implication that she or her campaign were in any way implicated in that," the South Dakota Republican told reporters. "This, to me, looks like a political hit job by a left-wing outlet that's trying to score points going into an election."

Much of Collins' reelection campaign was initially built around fighting Graham Platner, the oyster farmer who eventually dropped out amid a series of sexual misconduct allegations, which he denied. Troy Jackson, a logger and former president of the Maine state Senate, replaced Platner as the Democratic candidate whose name will be on the fall ballot.

In the day since the ProPublica story published, Jackson slammed his opponent over what he called "corruption of the highest order."

"We can’t afford six more years of being sold out to Trump and Collins’ corporate cronies," he wrote in a social media post.

Zachary Schermele is the congressional correspondent for USA TODAY. Reach him by email at zschermele@usatoday.com and on Signal @zachschermele.02. Follow him on X at @ZachSchermele.

title: Disgraced Theranos CEO Elizabeth Holmes approved for halfway house move in 2027
description:
Theranos founder and convicted felon Elizabeth Holmes has been approved for placement in a community correction center, or halfway house, and is scheduled to be placed there next year, according to an update from the Department of Justice's Victim Notification System, ABC News has learned.
Holmes is scheduled to be placed in the Austin Transitional Center in Del Valle, Texas, on Aug. 23, 2027, according to the notification.
Benjamin Fanjoy/Bloomberg via Getty Images - PHOTO: Elizabeth Holmes, founder of Theranos Inc., arrives at federal court in San Jose, Calif.
fullText:
Holmes is scheduled to be placed in the Austin Transitional Center.

Theranos founder and convicted felon Elizabeth Holmes has been approved for placement in a community correction center, or halfway house, and is scheduled to be placed there next year, according to an update from the Department of Justice's Victim Notification System, ABC News has learned.

Holmes is scheduled to be placed in the Austin Transitional Center in Del Valle, Texas, on Aug. 23, 2027, according to the notification.

When reached for comment on Wednesday, the Federal Bureau of Prisons said in a statement that it "does not discuss the conditions of confinement for any individual, including release plans."

"Additionally, per BOP policy, specific designation information cannot be released until after an individual arrives at their designated institution," the statement continued.

BOP said several factors go into assigning individuals to facilities, including "the level of security and supervision required, medical or programmatic needs, separation or security considerations necessary for the individual’s safety, and other relevant factors, such as proximity to the individual’s release residence."

Holmes was originally sentenced in 2022 to 11 years and 3 months in prison for defrauding investors with false claims about her company's blood-testing technology.

Her sentence has since been reduced to 10 years and 3 months, and she is now scheduled to be released on Feb. 22, 2030. According to the Victim Notification System, upon her release, Holmes will reside in Austin, Texas, and be supervised by the United States Probation Office there.

The new release date was the result of a retroactive change to federal sentencing guidelines and earned time through the First Step Act.

"To be clear, this sentence reduction does not diminish the enormity of Holmes's crimes, nor does it ignore the significant negative impact her conduct has had on the community," U.S. District Judge Edward Davila wrote in a March order granting a motion to reduce her sentence. "The hundreds of millions of dollars in losses caused by Holmes's fraud speak for themselves. And though unquantifiable, the echoes of the immense reputational damage that the innovative industry in Silicon Valley suffered as a consequence of Holmes's deception still reverberate to this day. Holmes's revised sentence continues to reflect a just punishment for her serious offense and serves as a reminder that the scales of justice will balance."

Holmes was found guilty of three counts of wire fraud and one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud while at the helm of Theranos. She reported to prison in May 2023.

Last year, a U.S. appeals court upheld the fraud convictions and $452 million restitution order for Holmes and her second-in-command, Ramesh "Sunny" Balwani.

The two had argued the court committed several legal errors and violated their constitutional rights during their separate trials. The three-judge panel for the appeals court rejected their claims, finding that any errors were harmless or that their arguments failed to show any violation.

Holmes is the subject of a forthcoming documentary by filmmaker Nathan Fielder, "You Can See Everything." In a new trailer for the film released Wednesday, Holmes maintained that she "did not" do anything wrong.

She participated in the documentary in 2023, before reporting to prison.

title: 8 sailors assigned to U.S. carrier group that fought in Iran war attempted suicide, Navy says
description: Aircraft on the deck of the US Navy Nimitz-class aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln as it docks for a rest stop at Laem Chabang Port, Thailand, on September 3, following a long deployment in the Middle East. - Chalinee...
fullText:
EDITOR’S NOTE:  This story contains discussion of suicide. Help is available if you or someone you know is struggling with suicidal thoughts or mental health matters. In the US, call or text 988 for help. The International Association for Suicide Prevention and Befrienders Worldwide have contact information for crisis centers around the world.

Eight US Navy personnel assigned to the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group attempted suicide during a period that included when the ships undertook combat operations against Iran and the carrier set a modern record for its time at sea, according to a letter from the service’s acting secretary, which was obtained by CNN.

Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao revealed the number, which has not been previously reported and covers crew members from several ships that travel together, including the carrier, in written responses to questions posed by Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand about the morale and mental health of the USS Abraham Lincoln’s crew. Cao wrote that no service members had killed themselves during the deployment.

The rate of suicide attempts among the Lincoln strike group’s sailors was roughly consistent with that of the entire active duty Navy in 2024, the most recent year for which the Pentagon has released suicide data. That year, the Navy saw 356 suicide attempts among its estimated 337,000 active duty sailors.

“Since the beginning of Lincoln’s deployment, there have been a total of eight suicide attempts across the strike group,” Cao wrote to Gillibrand, a Democrat and member of the Senate Armed Services, in a letter dated Tuesday. “This number includes the Lincoln crew and sailors from the carrier airwing, strike group and destroyer squadron staff, escorting destroyers and all embarked aviation squadrons.”

Between 6,000 and 7,000 US Navy sailors were deployed as part of the Lincoln strike group across roughly a half dozen ships — with the carrier kept out of port for over six months while conducting a high rate of combat operations against Iran.

“Eight attempted suicides is incredibly high,” one US military official told CNN, noting recent carrier strike group deployments have had one or two per year. “The strain of combat ops is much higher than normal deployments. No port calls, constant alerts, etc.”

The Navy did not respond ahead of publication to a request for comment about the letter.

“What Trump and Secretary Hegseth dismissed as ‘fake news’ turned out to be serious and deteriorating conditions for our service members,” Gillibrand said in a statement Wednesday to CNN. “Our troops and their families make immense sacrifices every single day, yet the president dismissed them with open disrespect. That this administration can find endless taxpayer dollars for bombs, ballrooms, and billionaires, but cannot take care of our service members, is completely unacceptable.”

The Lincoln deployed with various mental health resources onboard, including five chaplains, one embedded integrated prevention counselor, one psychologist, one clinical social worker, three behavioral health technicians and one expeditionary facility dog, according to Cao’s letter.

CNN previously reported that two sailors assigned to the Lincoln strike group, one from the carrier and one from another ship, had jumped overboard in recent months. Both were rescued, US officials said. Others were prevented from jumping, according to reports from the Navy Times and Stars and Stripes.

In his letter to Gillibrand, Cao also confirmed that a sailor assigned to the airwing went overboard from the ship in early August but was “quickly recovered” and treated by the Lincoln’s medical department. “Additionally, one sailor attempted to go overboard in March and was stopped by his shipmates. That sailor was also provided immediate medical care and subsequently returned to homeport.”

The Navy previously said in a statement to CNN, “We have not observed an increase in suicidal ideations or attempts aboard the ship. We take every service member’s well-being seriously and have religious, medical and mental health professionals available to assess and address concerns as they arise.”

A US official also previously told CNN that the Navy does not believe there is a correlation between deployment length and thoughts of self-harm, and that man overboard incidents are not unique to this group.

A crew member serving on the Lincoln previously described to CNN that morale on the carrier was very low and said they had heard repeatedly about suicidal ideation by fellow crew members. And there were regular strains on essential amenities — toilets and water fountains around the ship frequently closed, and hot water was often unavailable, the crew member said.

“Everyday we wake up and listen to our captain speak, we are desperately hoping and anxious for updates on our return,” the crew member, speaking before the ship had been ordered to return to its home port in San Diego, told CNN. The ship left the Middle East in August and is expected back in San Diego in the coming weeks.

Other sailors aboard the Lincoln who spoke with CNN described conditions unlike their prior deployments, largely due to the combat that has kept the carrier from making stops at friendly ports. Ships can take on new supplies and allow their sailors to rest and relax during those port calls.

This story has been updated with additional details.

CNN’s Davis Winkie and Pamela Brown contributed to this report

fullText:
Donna Ganger, the mother of Renee Good, who was fatally shot by a federal immigration officer in Minneapolis earlier this year, said Tuesday she voted for President Trump and thought that federal immigration officers would “protect” Americans.

Ganger said it is “torture” that “as a mom and as a family, we could not protect” Good, who was killed by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer on Jan. 7 in an incident caught on video that triggered a nationwide discussion on the Trump administration’s immigration efforts.

“But no one can protect against others who are determined to disregard our country’s constitutional rules and values,” Good’s mother added. She spoke during a public forum hosted by Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) and Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.).

“I’m a registered Republican,” Ganger said. “I voted for President Trump under the impression that these agents were here to protect the citizens of the United States, innocents like our family and the others here, against terrorists, certainly not to accuse those of us here of being terrorists and take precious lives.”

After the officer fatally shot Good, a 37-year-old American citizen with one son, multiple Trump administration officials said the woman committed “domestic terrorism” by allegedly driving her car toward the ICE officer.

“This was an act of domestic terrorism,” then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem said in January.

Video taken by the officer on his cellphone, though, appears to show Good turning her car away from him before the fatal shots were fired.

The incident, along with the fatal shooting of 37-year-old Alex Pretti by Customs and Border Protection (CBP) agents Raymundo Gutierrez and Jesus Ochoa later that month, sparked backlash to the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown in Minneapolis.

Blumenthal said Wednesday that Congress “must hold” ICE and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) “accountable” for deaths involving federal personnel.

“Totally unacceptable that there has been no real investigation into DHS/ICE related deaths & injuries,” Blumenthal wrote on the social platform X.

The Hill has reached out to DHS, ICE and CBP for the latest on the investigations into the killings of Good and Pretti.
